The authors test whether connections to a focal provincial government help, connections to rival provincial governments hurt (especially when rivalry is intense), and whether ties to the central government can neutralize negative effects. The study’s main contribution is showing that political connections can be both assets and liabilities simultaneously, even in stable regimes, due to intergovernmental rivalry.

Workplace helping is essential for organizational and economic success, yet it may decline during difficult economic periods when it is most needed. Existing research has not adequately explained how macroeconomic conditions influence individual employee behaviors like helping. This study addresses that gap by investigating whether and how economic downturns reduce workplace helping. The authors propose that cues of economic downturns trigger a zero-sum construal of success, leading employees to perceive others' success as a threat to their own, thereby reducing helping—even when helping entails no personal cost. The research uses multiple methods including cross-national surveys, experiments, and field data. It contributes by bridging the macro-micro divide in organizational research and showing how broader economic signals shape core workplace behaviors.

Global mobility is central to multinational corporations, yet repatriate career success remains poorly understood and managed. While some repatriates advance, others face stagnation, and systematic research on what drives these differing outcomes is scarce. This study addresses the gap by integrating traditional career theory—which emphasizes organizational support and human capital—and protean career theory—which emphasizes individual self-direction—to explain objective and subjective repatriate career success. Using survey data from 295 German repatriates and PLS-SEM analysis, the study tests how assignment purpose, performance, destination, organizational support, and self-directed career management affect career outcomes. It contributes by showing that both organizational and individual factors matter, laying the groundwork for more holistic repatriation strategies.

Interdisciplinary research faces two major challenges: cognitive differences in knowledge and methods across disciplines, and political economy systems that reward disciplinary work. These barriers create both knowledge transfer costs and career risks for researchers. Existing solutions focus on one issue or the other, but few address both simultaneously. This paper asks how cognitive and political boundaries are spanned together in interdisciplinary research. Drawing on a field study of a nanotechnology research center, we examine how students and scientific instruments interact to enable collaboration. The approach centers on symbiont practices—mutual engagements between students and instruments—as the core mechanism. The key contribution is revealing how material and human affordances combine in practice to overcome both cognitive and political barriers at once.

Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often rely on informal human resource management (HRM) practices due to resource constraints, and the performance effects of high-performance work systems (HPWSs) in these contexts are mixed. While prior research has established positive links between HPWSs and performance in larger firms, less is known about boundary conditions in SMEs, particularly the role of formal HR departments. The gap this study addresses is whether the existence of an HR department strengthens the HPWS–performance relationship in SMEs, given that HR departments may enhance implementation quality and system coherence. The research investigates this interaction using data from 125 U.S. small and medium-sized establishments from the 2002 National Organizations Survey. The approach uses an AMO (ability, motivation, opportunity) framework and tests for moderating effects. The key contribution claimed is identifying HR department presence as a significant moderator of HPWS effectiveness on perceived labor productivity in SMEs.

Teams are expected to enhance creativity through knowledge sharing, such as advice-giving, yet prior research shows mixed effects where advice-giving sometimes fails to increase creativity or even harms the giver’s creative output. A key gap is understanding why some advice-giving behaviors are more creatively beneficial than others. This study argues that the advice giver’s network position—specifically their brokerage in the team’s advice-giving network—is a critical factor. It posits that brokers provide more non-redundant information, enhancing recipients’ creativity, and that these recipient gains subsequently boost the giver’s own creativity. The study uses a longitudinal design with network analysis and integrates psychological safety as a boundary condition. The key contribution is clarifying advice-giving as a brokerage-driven, socially perpetuated phenomenon in teams.

Negative mentoring experiences, such as interpersonal problems, are common and can harm mentors' well-being, yet little research has explored their impact on work-family conflict (WFC). While prior studies link mentoring to positive outcomes, mentors may suffer psychological costs, especially emotional exhaustion, due to resource depletion. This study addresses the gap by investigating how interpersonal problems contribute to WFC through emotional exhaustion, drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory. It also examines revenge as a moderator, asking whether retaliating against protégés worsens or alleviates these effects. Using a field survey of 187 Chinese mentors, the study employs a moderated mediation model. It contributes by identifying emotional exhaustion as a key mechanism and revenge as a boundary condition, offering new insight into the dark side of mentoring.

title: 10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.01.006
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

entries.rq_with_context: Leader humility has been widely viewed as beneficial for followers and organizations, yet its consequences for leaders themselves remain underexplored. While prior research emphasizes the positive relational aspects of humility, there is limited understanding of potential downsides when humility may undermine perceptions of leader competence and control. Drawing on leader categorization theory, this paper investigates the dual impact of humility on how leaders are perceived along communal (e.g., warm, cooperative) and agentic (e.g., skillful, decisive) dimensions—both of which are important for leadership judgments. The research uses five experimental studies to test whether humility’s benefit in boosting communal perceptions is counterbalanced by its cost in reducing agentic perceptions, ultimately affecting leader effectiveness and undermining behaviors. The central contribution lies in demonstrating mutual suppression: that humility's indirect effects operate through two opposing pathways.

The paper investigates how pervasive Western organizational mentalities—particularly linear clock-time orientation—shape market-based models for human development. While such temporal structures enhance efficiency and control in markets, they may be ill-suited for managing the emergent, complex, and indeterminate processes characteristic of development work. The authors study Fairtrade International, an organization connecting Northern markets with Southern producers, to understand intra-organizational contestation over different temporal structures needed to align with discrepant temporal environments. Drawing on ethnographic data, they ask how organizations navigate conflict between linear, outcome-oriented market timelines and processual, context-dependent development rhythms. Using a framework of temporal structuring and process theory, the study reveals how contestation, temporal reflexivity, and mutual appreciation of interdependencies enable change. The authors' primary contribution is to advance theory on time in organizations by proposing an agentic view of temporality and introducing the concept of 'ambitemporality' to explain how organizations can hold multiple, seemingly contradictory temporal orientations.

title: 10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.11.002
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

entries.rq_with_context: Chronic absenteeism in preschools—especially those serving low-income families—is a persistent problem with consequences for children, peers, and schools, and is often linked to structural barriers such as illness or transportation. However, the study identifies a gap in understanding the role of malleable parental factors, such as beliefs about the importance of preschool and expectations for attendance, especially given the voluntary nature of preschool compared to compulsory kindergarten. The research asks whether a low-cost behavioral intervention—sending personalized text messages to parents—can reduce absenteeism by targeting these cognitive and motivational factors. Using a randomized controlled trial across nine Chicago preschool centers, the authors test the impact of messages focused on goal setting, planning prompts, and correcting misbeliefs. The study contributes evidence that such a light-touch intervention can meaningfully increase attendance, particularly among those with the highest baseline levels of absenteeism.

title: 10.1016/j.obhdp.2016.04.006
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

entries.rq_with_context: Although people generally value personal choice, they may avoid making decisions for others due to anticipated responsibility and blame if outcomes are poor. Prior research has not clearly examined whether delegation is uniquely driven by the desire to avoid responsibility, rather than difficulty or lack of concern. This paper investigates whether people are more likely to delegate choices for others than for themselves, particularly when outcomes are potentially negative, and whether this tendency is specifically due to a desire to avoid blame and responsibility. The authors use a series of experiments involving real or hypothetical decisions affecting oneself or another person. They find that delegation is more common for others, uniquely serves to absolve responsibility, and is limited to surrogates who can assume blame, regardless of expertise.

Organizations increasingly rely on employees to engage in organizational citizenship behaviors (OCB) to maintain effectiveness, yet economic pressures have heightened job insecurity, creating tension. Prior research reports inconsistent findings—negative, positive, or null—on the link between job insecurity and OCB, suggesting the relationship may be complex. This study proposes a U-shaped curvilinear relationship to explain these mixed results, drawing on social exchange theory and personal control research. It investigates whether employees reduce OCB at moderate insecurity due to weakened reciprocity but increase OCB at high insecurity to regain control through obligation. Using a sample of Chinese employees, the authors test this using hierarchical linear modeling and examine psychological capital and subordinate–supervisor guanxi as moderators. The authors claim their work advances understanding by identifying a nonlinear pattern and highlighting proactive employee responses to extreme job insecurity.

Science commercialization has been widely studied for its empirical relationships, but less attention has been paid to its potential for generating theoretical contributions to general management. While existing research has documented technology transfer and academic entrepreneurship, there is a gap in understanding how this context’s distinct characteristics can inform broader theoretical development. The paper asks how science commercialization, as a rich and complex context, can be used to build management theory. It focuses on two underexplored facets: the process of transitioning across institutional boundaries (e.g., academic to commercial) and the variety of goals and impacts among stakeholders. Using a review of management literature, the authors frame science commercialization as a 'living lab' for theory-building and propose a research agenda. Their key contribution is reframing this context not just as a subject of study, but as a generator of generalizable theoretical insights for management.

Existing research on international coercion often assumes that coercers can influence targets through direct resource dependence. However, less is known about how coercers exert influence when targets are not directly dependent on them. This paper addresses that gap by analyzing a case in which U.S. authorities pressured Swiss policymakers to change national banking secrecy laws, despite lacking direct leverage over the Swiss state. The authors introduce 'indirect compellence' as a novel mechanism where coercers threaten a third party—Swiss banks—to induce compliance from the actual target. Drawing on a qualitative case study of U.S.-Swiss conflict over tax evasion, the paper investigates how Swiss policymakers’ political ideologies shaped their interpretations of coercive threats. The study uses a constructivist, target-centered approach to explain variation in compliance, offering a nuanced understanding of power in international institutional change.

Many employees experience unfair treatment from their supervisors and often respond by discussing it with coworkers. Conventional wisdom suggests such talk is beneficial, helping employees make sense of the experience and "let off steam." However, existing research may not fully capture the long-term emotional and relational consequences of these conversations. This study identifies a gap in understanding whether unfairness talk ultimately helps employees move on or prolongs negative outcomes. Drawing on cognitive-motivational-relational theory, the authors ask how unfairness talk influences emotions like anger and hope, and in turn, forgiveness and citizenship behavior. They use a two-study approach—a field study with bus drivers and a lab experiment—to test these relationships. The research contributes by challenging the assumption that talking about unfairness is always helpful and by revealing the moderating role of coworker responses.

Individuals are inherently multidimensional, carrying bundles of attributes and social relations that influence their experiences in organizations. Despite growing research, multidimensionality studies remain fragmented across disconnected literatures—intersectionality, faultlines, and multiplexity—each focusing on different aspects: social identities from attribute intersections, group dividing lines based on attribute alignment, and overlapping social relationships, respectively. This fragmentation limits a holistic understanding of how multidimensionality shapes organizational outcomes. This paper reviews and integrates these three literatures to provide a comprehensive overview of their theoretical foundations, measurement approaches, and current empirical findings. The research aims to identify pathways for integrating these perspectives and offers future research directions. The primary contribution is a unified framework that bridges diversity and social network views of multidimensionality, enabling more nuanced inquiry into its effects across individual, group, and organizational levels.

The paper addresses the lack of research on shared perceptions of work meaningfulness in teams, despite growing interest in meaningful work at the individual level. While leadership is known to shape team climate, little is known about how spiritual leadership specifically influences meaningfulness climate and subsequent team outcomes. The study fills this gap by investigating how spiritual leaders foster a shared belief that work is significant and valuable, thereby enhancing team effectiveness in terms of performance and OCB. Drawing on social information processing theory, the authors propose that team members rely more on spiritual leaders for meaning-making under high task uncertainty. The study uses a three-wave, multisource survey of 123 teams in China to test a moderated mediation model. The key contribution is demonstrating that spiritual leadership improves team effectiveness through meaningfulness climate, especially when task uncertainty is high.

Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has transitioned from a debated organizational obligation into a mainstream practice, with increasing academic and managerial attention. Despite extensive research, there remains a need to understand the underlying complexities of how firms organize and manage CSR, particularly regarding stakeholder interdependencies, motives for compliance versus commitment, and the influence of institutional environments. This editorial reviews 87 CSR-related articles published in the Academy of Management Journal (AMJ) from 1958 to 2015 to trace thematic shifts and identify underexplored areas. It uses content analysis across decades to map trends in focus—such as the shift from financial to non-financial outcomes and from aggregate CSR measures to specific dimensions—and highlights emerging patterns in global and micro-level analysis. The primary contribution is a structured overview that identifies key gaps and proposes concrete directions for future CSR research.

Employee engagement has become a popular construct in organizational research, yet concerns about the validity of its measurement persist, particularly regarding the widely used Utrecht Work Engagement Scale (UWES). While the UWES dominates the field, it has been criticized for overlapping with other constructs like burnout and job attitudes. The Job Engagement Scale (JES), based on Kahn’s self-role-expression theory, offers a different conceptualization, but no study has rigorously compared both measures. This paper addresses this gap by examining the factor structure and nomological network of both scales across five field samples. The research asks whether the UWES and JES measure the same construct and how engagement, as a construct, relates to burnout, commitment, and psychological meaningfulness when measurement error is controlled. The study uses confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling to assess construct validity. It contributes by clarifying conceptual and measurement issues in engagement research and offering guidance on when to use each scale.

Rising societal income inequality has prompted debate over the role of firms in shaping wage distributions. Cobb (2016) argues that a shift from organizational to market-based employment, driven by political dynamics, has eroded internal pay systems that previously moderated inequality. However, Zardkoohi and Bierman contest this, pointing to established organizational compensation systems—seniority-based pay, efficiency wages, and tournament pay—that inherently produce greater internal pay disparity than external markets. Using transaction cost economics as a theoretical foundation, they argue that boundary choices between internal and external operations are driven primarily by efficiency considerations, not politics. They claim that moving work to the market, where pay is more closely tied to performance, would actually reduce overall pay inequality. Their contribution lies in challenging a politically centered explanation with an institutional economic framework that emphasizes structural and incentive-based forces within organizations.

The implementation of HRM practices by line managers is critical for translating intended HR systems into actual employee experiences and outcomes. While prior research has focused on the extent to which line managers implement HR practices (the 'what'), less attention has been paid to the 'how'—specifically, the process of balancing consistent treatment of all team members with responsiveness to individual differences. This study addresses this gap by investigating two seemingly contradictory dimensions of HRM implementation: consistency (treating team members uniformly) and individual responsiveness (considering individual contributions). The research question is how these dimensions, both individually and in combination, affect individual job performance and team viability. Using a multilevel design with data from 60 consulting project teams, the study applies paradox theory to frame these dimensions as interrelated rather than opposing. The key claimed contribution is demonstrating that these paradoxical practices can be managed synergistically, with consistency strengthening the positive effect of individual responsiveness on individual job performance.

title: 10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.01.005
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

entries.rq_with_context: Individuals often face situations where they must disclose negative information (e.g., weaknesses in job interviews), which can harm perceptions of competence and warmth. While prior research has examined disclosure likelihood, little work has explored how such disclosures are perceived. This study addresses that gap by examining humor’s role in impression management. It asks whether using humor during negative disclosures changes how truthful those disclosures seem and, consequently, how the discloser is judged. The authors use the Speaker's Inferred Motive (SIM) Model, drawing on linguistic theory and Benign Violation Theory, to propose that humor signals an entertainment motive, reducing perceived veracity of proximal statements. The key contribution is demonstrating that humor can mitigate the reputational costs of self-disclosure by making negative claims seem less true.

Transnational knowledge-intensive service firms face a coordination problem: how to balance standardized work with non-routine adaptation across locations. While existing research highlights challenges of cross-border coordination, few studies explore how professionals actually enact services transnationally from a knowledge-in-practice perspective. This article analyzes empirical data from two engineering firms to understand how services are coordinated through patterns of action. The research focuses on two questions: how prefigured and emergent practices are enacted, and what kinds of knowledge are involved. Using practice theory, it examines everyday activities to uncover the practical accomplishment of coordination. The study contributes by showing how balanced acting between routine and adaptive work enables transnational service delivery.

Organizations often operate under institutional complexity, where multiple, divergent logics (like social and commercial) create internal tensions, especially during periods of environmental turbulence such as economic crises. While prior research identifies collaboration and formalization as mechanisms to manage these tensions, it remains unclear how they interact to reconcile conflicting demands. This study asks how organizations originally guided by a central logic change when turbulence amplifies a competing, peripheral logic. Based on a longitudinal, inductive study of four social enterprises during the 2008 financial crisis, the authors develop a process model. They show that the structured interaction between formalization and collaboration, rather than either mechanism alone, allows organizations to successfully blend logics and reconcile tensions, with the sequence of these processes being critical to the outcome.

The phenomenon of interest is how knowledge characteristics influence individual creativity over time. While existing research suggests both knowledge depth and breadth foster creativity, empirical findings are mixed, possibly because they do not account for where individuals are in their careers. This study addresses the gap by proposing that as career age increases, knowledge structures become more rigid, changing how knowledge depth and breadth affect creativity. The research question is whether knowledge depth is more beneficial early in a career when knowledge complexity is needed, while breadth becomes more beneficial later when flexibility is needed. The authors use a longitudinal design in the Hollywood animation industry, leveraging archival data on creators' careers and awards. The key claimed contribution is resolving inconsistencies in the knowledge-creativity literature by showing the contingent role of career age.

Idiosyncratic deals (i-deals) are personalized work arrangements that employees negotiate with employers, increasingly used to attract and retain talent, especially in jobs requiring creativity. While prior research has focused on social exchange theory to explain i-deals’ effects, this study identifies a gap in understanding internal motivational mechanisms. Drawing on social cognitive theory, the authors investigate whether creative self-efficacy (CSE) mediates the relationship between developmental and flexibility i-deals and employee creativity. They test this using survey data from 177 employees in R&D organizations in China. The study contributes by introducing CSE as a mediating mechanism and distinguishing between two types of i-deals, offering new insight into how customized work arrangements influence creativity.

The paper addresses the ongoing critique that management theory, while rigorous, often lacks practical relevance. Despite high standards in theoretical development, especially in journals like the Academy of Management Review (AMR), most theoretical work has limited influence on actual managerial practice. The gap lies in the tendency of theory journals to prioritize novel constructs over theories grounded in real-world organizational phenomena. The paper challenges the one-way model of knowledge transfer—from academics to practitioners—and instead proposes that theory should emerge from practice. It uses examples like Peters and Waterman’s work on culture, paradoxical organizing, and the invention of Post-it Notes to show how practice has historically inspired theory. The approach is conceptual and reflective, calling for 'phenomenal theory'—theory rooted in observable, impactful practices. The key contribution is reframing Lewin’s maxim to argue that good practice is itself deeply theoretical and should be the starting point for academic theorizing.

While work–family boundary research is well established, little attention has been paid to non-family roles like volunteering, despite calls to expand the work–life domain. This gap marginalizes important life enrichment roles and limits understanding of how individuals manage multiple, overlapping role demands. This study addresses that gap by exploring how volunteers communicatively manage role interfaces involving work, personal, and volunteer roles. Using qualitative interviews with 38 participants, the study applies a hermeneutic phenomenological and communicative social constructionist lens to uncover lived experiences of boundary management. The authors identify new processes—specifically boundary collapsing—and show that individuals shift between strategies depending on context. This contributes to theory by expanding the integration–segmentation framework and emphasizing boundary management as a dynamic, communicative process.

Despite extensive research on CEO labor markets, little is known about factors influencing non-CEO executive advancement. Similarly, while board directorship roles are well studied, the motivations for executives to serve on boards remain unclear. This study addresses both gaps by examining how board service affects non-CEO executives' career outcomes. It proposes that board appointments serve as third-party certifications of executive quality and enhance human and social capital, thereby improving labor market prospects. Using propensity score matching on a longitudinal sample of 2,104 top U.S. executives from 1996 to 2012, the study tests whether first-time board appointments increase the likelihood of CEO promotion (inside and outside the firm), other promotions, and higher pay. The key contribution is demonstrating that board service provides tangible career benefits, advancing understanding of both executive advancement and director motivation.

Financial misconduct at one firm may negatively affect the market valuations of other firms in the same industry, but little is known about whether this contamination occurs heterogeneously or what factors influence investor perceptions. Existing research has focused primarily on the direct effects of misconduct on the offending firms themselves or on non-financial scandals like product recalls, leaving a gap in understanding how financial wrongdoing triggers broader market reactions. This study investigates how industry bystander firms are affected when financial misconduct is revealed, focusing on the mechanisms of generalization (extending culpability to the industry category) and instantiation (perceptions that specific firms embody that culpability). Using a sample of 725 firms across 84 restatement events, the authors apply a social cognition lens rooted in categorization and attribution theory. They find that contamination occurs heterogeneously and is shaped by perpetrator familiarity, governance cues, and firm size, contributing to research on investor behavior, corporate governance, and organizational misconduct.

Regulatory focus theory distinguishes between promotion (growth, accomplishments) and prevention (duty, safety) motivational systems. While widely studied at the individual level, a growing body of work explores its application across multiple levels of organizations. Despite meta-analyses on individual outcomes, key gaps remain about how regulatory focus operates in multilevel contexts, particularly how individuals adapt their focus to situational demands and how teams develop collective regulatory focus. The paper asks: How do regulatory focus dynamics—especially regulatory fit and hierarchical shifts between chronic and state focus—function across individual, team, and organizational levels? Using a multilevel framework, the review synthesizes research from organizational behavior, HR, entrepreneurship, and strategy, with an emphasis on contextual adjustments in motivation. The primary contribution is an integrative model highlighting research gaps in collective and multilevel regulatory processes.

Low-skilled workers and immigrants face high health risks due to poor working conditions, social isolation, and limited access to health interventions. Despite the potential of organizational interventions, few are designed for this group, especially with attention to participation barriers. This study evaluates a peer-mentoring intervention implemented via nonprofit health agencies to improve social support and health. Using a realist evaluation framework, it investigates five proposed mechanisms of change across three companies over six months. The research asks whether peer-mentor and line manager support increased, and whether this led to improved health outcomes like reduced blood pressure and psychosomatic complaints. It contributes by testing a theory-driven intervention tailored to a high-risk, under-served group.

Organizations today increasingly grapple with hybridity—combining social and business missions, multiple institutional logics, or conflicting demands within a single entity. While prior research has examined short-term strategies for managing such tensions, less is known about how hybridity is sustained over time, especially as environmental shifts, stakeholder pressures, and internal conflicts persist. The literature lacks an in-depth understanding of the long-term processes organizations use to avoid mission drift or collapse. This paper addresses that gap by studying the first ten years of Digital Divide Data (DDD), a successful social enterprise. The research asks: How do organizations sustain hybridity over time? Drawing on longitudinal qualitative data, the authors identify a model of structured flexibility—combining stable organizational features and adaptive enactment processes—as key to sustaining dual missions. The contribution is reorienting hybridity research from isolated strategies to the interaction of stability and adaptation.

Managerial risk taking is critical for strategic management, as top managers must navigate uncertainty to improve competitive advantage and performance. While agency theory suggests aligning managerial and shareholder interests through incentives to encourage risk taking, other theories challenge this view by emphasizing psychological, behavioral, and contextual factors. Despite extensive research on individual theories, there remains a lack of integration across theoretical perspectives, limiting our understanding of how different mechanisms interact in shaping managerial risk-taking behaviors. This review addresses that gap by synthesizing research across five key theories—agency theory, behavioral theory of the firm, prospect theory, behavioral agency model, and upper echelons theory—to examine both individual and organizational drivers of managerial risk taking. The authors use a comprehensive literature review to map out antecedents, moderators, and outcomes of risk-taking behaviors, and propose a framework (Figure 1) that integrates these perspectives. The primary contribution is a cross-theoretical research agenda that highlights inconsistencies, boundary conditions, and opportunities for future research on managerial risk taking.

The paper investigates relational attributions in interdependent work relationships, where one member receives negative performance feedback. Attribution theory traditionally distinguishes between internal (personal) and external (situational) causes, but prior research has suggested a third, relational locus of causality—where the cause lies in the relationship itself. However, there is little empirical evidence on whether people spontaneously make such attributions or what their consequences are. This study fills that gap by testing when relational attributions occur and how they are linked to relational improvement behaviors. Using Kelley’s covariation model (consistency, distinctiveness, consensus), the authors predict that relational attributions are more likely under conditions of high consistency, high distinctiveness, and low consensus. They also examine personal, relational, and contextual moderators. The research uses quantitative and qualitative data from seven samples across three studies and contributes evidence that relational attributions are distinct and impactful, especially when employees share the same sex and perceive sufficient time and energy for relationship repair.

Grappa was historically a low-status spirit, consumed by peasants and alpine soldiers and associated with artisanal, even clandestine production. Despite efforts to improve quality, it remained institutionally locked in a low-status position compared to cognac and whisky. The phenomenon under study is the radical recategorization of grappa from a marginalized drink to a high-status cultural symbol. The gap lies in understanding how such vertical status change can occur in mature fields where status imperatives resist change, especially when the category itself—not just individual organizations within it—undergoes status elevation. Prior studies focus on organizational status or horizontal category creation, not vertical category recategorization. We use a historical case study of the Nonino family's efforts to reposition grappa, analyzing archival and interview data. Our contribution is identifying 'theorization by allusion'—a process using detachment, emulation, and sublimation—as a novel mechanism that enables status recategorization by avoiding direct contestation.

Firefighting is a high-risk, interdependent occupation where trust is essential, yet direct experience fighting fires is extremely rare—only about 4 percent of calls involve actual fires. This creates a critical gap: firefighters must trust others in life-or-death situations without sufficient domain-specific evidence. While trust research has focused on knowledge-based evidence (e.g., competence, experience), the role of faith—making trust judgments beyond available evidence—remains poorly understood. This study investigates how firefighters overcome this by making and sustaining 'leaps of faith.' Using a multi-phase, inductive qualitative approach, the authors identify the social and occupational processes that support and sustain trust under uncertainty. The research contributes by uncovering how faith, not just evidence, enables trust in extreme conditions.

The article investigates how organizations manage dissonance between their claimed identity and external reputation, focusing on a large consulting firm where such misalignment is common. While prior research suggests identity threats lead to internal re-evaluation or change, this study finds the firm does not alter its core identity despite reputational gaps. Instead, the research asks how such identity-reputation conflicts are managed in practice. It uses a case study approach to document the mechanisms used to remediate reputation conflicts through individual-level identity work. The authors argue that the firm buffers organizational identity from change by shifting attention to individual consultants' reputations, enacting thought leadership, and emphasizing extra value in client engagements.

Knowledge-intensive teamwork, such as in R&D teams, is central to innovation and competitive advantage, yet little is known about the organizational conditions that support it. While HRM systems are recognized as a driver of employee behaviors in strategic HRM research, their impact on team-level knowledge activities remains underexplored, especially in combination with task and leadership factors. This study addresses this gap by examining how firm-level HRM systems affect team knowledge acquisition and team knowledge sharing in 162 R&D teams. Using a multilevel framework, it tests whether knowledge tacitness and empowering leadership moderate these relationships. The authors claim the study contributes to strategic HRM by integrating multilevel analysis and specifying boundary conditions for HRM effectiveness in knowledge-intensive settings.

Since the 2004 publication of 'Understanding HRM-firm performance linkages,' the concept of HRM system strength has gained influence in strategic HRM research. This construct was introduced to explain how HR processes—distinct from practices—affect employee sense-making by creating strong situations that lead to shared climate perceptions. However, subsequent research has often misapplied the construct by treating it as an individual-level perceptual variable rather than a higher-level organizational property. There is growing confusion over how HRM system strength should be conceptualized and measured, with many studies relying on indirect proxies such as aggregated practice scores or employee-manager alignment. The authors aim to clarify the original intent of the construct, review its application, and identify persistent gaps in theory and measurement that hinder its full potential. Their approach draws on attribution theory, communication theory, and Mischel’s strong situations framework to reassert HRM system strength as a contextual, multi-source phenomenon. The key contribution is a critical reflection that redirects future research toward proper conceptualization, higher-level operationalization, and theoretical refinement of HRM system strength.

Transgender employees often face stigma and discrimination at work, and the decision to express a stigmatized identity like gender identity is typically fraught with concern over negative consequences. While prior research has linked identity expression to positive job outcomes, the psychological mechanisms behind these effects remain unclear. This study addresses that gap by testing whether authenticity—specifically, feeling that one’s outward gender expression matches one’s inner identity (action authenticity) and feeling that others perceive one consistently with that identity (relational authenticity)—explains why greater gender transition is associated with better job satisfaction, higher perceived person-organization fit, and lower perceived discrimination. Using two studies with transgender employees, the authors apply Kernis’s (2003) model of authenticity to test these mediating mechanisms. The work contributes by identifying authenticity as a key psychological process underlying identity expression outcomes.

Youth joblessness is known to have long-term scarring effects on employment and income, but less is known about how these effects differ across ethnic and gender lines. While existing research shows ethnic minorities face labour market disadvantages, it often relies on cross-sectional data and does not track how early non-employment affects later outcomes. This paper addresses that gap by investigating how early labour market experiences (at ages 16–29 in 2001) influence employment probabilities 10 years later for second-generation ethnic minorities compared to white British individuals. Using longitudinal census data (ONS Longitudinal Study), the study examines variations by ethnicity (Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Caribbean, white British) and gender. The analysis employs logistic regression with controls for social origin and neighbourhood deprivation. The authors claim their findings reveal nuanced patterns of scarring, challenging assumptions that ethnic minorities uniformly suffer greater disadvantages.

The contemporary 'new career' perspective emphasizes individual agency in managing one's career, yet there is limited understanding of how career self-management interacts with organizational support across different life stages. While existing research often treats career management as universally effective regardless of age, little attention has been paid to how aging and shifting motivational goals may change the effectiveness of self-management strategies. This study addresses this gap by investigating how the interaction between career self-management, developmental HR practices, and perceived organizational support shapes career satisfaction differently for young and middle-aged employees. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) and socioemotional selectivity (SES) theories, the study uses time-lagged data from 364 Japanese employees. The key contribution is demonstrating that age changes whether organizational support enhances or diminishes the impact of self-management on satisfaction.

The paper addresses the widespread narrative that women have uniquely dysfunctional same-sex workplace relationships, evident in media coverage and research on phenomena like the queen bee syndrome. Despite evidence that men and women do not differ significantly in indirect aggression, female conflict is disproportionately criticized. The authors identify a gap in understanding whether this negative perception arises from actual behavioral differences or from biased interpretations by third parties. They propose a two-stage theory: first, women may experience more same-sex conflict due to competitive and collective threat; second, female same-sex conflict is more problematized because it violates gender stereotypes. Using social comparison and attribution theory, they frame conflict perception as shaped by prescriptive gender norms. The claimed contribution is a unified theory explaining both possible causes and the social amplification of female same-sex conflict, offering a framework to critically assess gendered assumptions in organizational research.

Managers are often incentivized with stock options to make long-term investments like R&D and CAPX, which have uncertain future returns. However, prior research suggests that managers believe the stock market reacts positively to R&D in the short term but not to CAPX, creating asymmetric incentives. This paper investigates whether the timing of option exercisability—when managers can actually cash out—affects how they allocate resources between these two types of investment. The research question is whether unexercisable (long-term) versus exercisable (short-term) stock options differentially influence changes in R&D and CAPX spending. Using a behavioral agency framework, the study analyzes over 6,500 firm-year observations from U.S. manufacturing firms. The authors claim their findings reveal that option incentives can lead to resource allocation decisions that benefit managers personally, even when misaligned with optimal firm performance.

Entrepreneurs are known to differ from other professionals in their cognition and behavior, and recent research highlights how identity shapes entrepreneurial actions. However, little is known about how multiple, within-individual role identities—such as entrepreneur, manager, and investor—affect opportunity evaluation and selection. While prior research often treats entrepreneurs as having a singular identity, this study addresses the gap by exploring how shifting role identities lead to different cognitive patterns in the same individual. The research question is: How do differences in role identities influence how entrepreneurs think about—and select—opportunities? Using verbal protocol and content analysis with founder entrepreneurs, the study investigates cognition across three role-primed decision scenarios. The authors claim this work contributes by showing that role identity, not just personal traits, shapes entrepreneurial decisions, and that risk perception and opportunity focus are situationally dependent on the 'hat' an entrepreneur is wearing.

Despite ongoing underrepresentation of women in senior leadership—especially in male-dominated sectors like accounting and finance—many executive women continue to deny gender inequality and individualize career challenges. Existing research has documented how neoliberalism promotes discourses of individualization and repudiation of structural barriers, but less attention has been paid to the deeper, unconscious reasons why women remain emotionally invested in these seemingly contradictory positions. This article addresses this gap by applying psychosocial theory, specifically Melanie Klein’s concepts of splitting and blaming, to understand how executive women manage anxiety provoked by the dissonance between lived experience and neoliberal ideals. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 36 women executives, the study explores how they unconsciously split off negative experiences and blame other women to preserve a belief in a fair, meritocratic workplace. The contribution lies in explaining the psychic mechanisms behind women's disavowal of gender discrimination, thus extending postfeminist and organizational scholarship on the subjectivities fostered under neoliberalism.

Cross-border acquisitions (CBAs) are a major international growth strategy, yet many fail to deliver value. While prior research has focused on host country factors and cultural distance, this study addresses a key underexplored question: how do acquirers’ home country institutions shape postacquisition performance? Existing research has not fully theorized or tested the direct impact of home country institutions, despite evidence that national context constrains managerial behavior. This paper fills that gap by proposing that informal institutions (collectivism and humane orientation) facilitate integration by fostering interdependence, while formal institutions (shareholder orientation and property rights protection) may hinder it by emphasizing ownership and short-term value extraction. Using a multilevel analysis of 12,021 CBAs from 41 countries, the study tests how these institutions individually and jointly affect long-term performance. It contributes by showing that home country institutional context directly shapes acquisition outcomes, especially through the interplay between formal and informal institutions.

Workplace helping is essential in interdependent, innovative environments where employees encounter unpredictable challenges and knowledge gaps. While existing research focuses on individual motivations for deciding to help or seek help—often framing it as a costly exchange—this study identifies a gap in understanding how helping actually unfolds over time, especially in contexts where helping is routine rather than exceptional. The authors ask: How does helping behavior unfold in organizations doing innovative work? Using ethnographic data from a high-tech firm, they apply an organizational routines lens to reveal the processual nature of helping. Their analysis shows that helping is not just a one-time decision but a recurrent, interdependent process driven by joint cognitive and emotional engagement. The key contribution is reframing helping as a collective routine rather than a dyadic exchange, highlighting how it enables coordination in uncertain environments.

Although creativity is widely believed to enhance performance, empirical evidence is limited, and prior research often conflates creativity with performance. A key debate centers on whether extrinsic rewards support or undermine creativity, given its presumed intrinsic motivation. This study addresses this by investigating how the perception of being rewarded for creativity influences the expression of creativity—specifically, the balance between novelty and usefulness—and how that, in turn, affects job performance. Using a sample of 310 employees and 50 supervisors, the authors apply motivated information processing and agency theories to test their hypotheses. They argue their contribution lies in showing that reward for creativity does not simply increase or decrease creativity, but changes which dimension—novelty or usefulness—is more strongly tied to performance.

title: 10.1016/j.obhdp.2015.08.004
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

entries.rq_with_context: The left-digit effect (LDE) refers to the tendency of individuals to overweight the leftmost digit when comparing numerical values, such as prices ending in .99 versus whole dollars. While prior research has documented this bias in pricing and financial decision-making, existing theories do not explain how emotional or motivational factors like loss aversion might modulate its strength. This paper identifies a gap in understanding whether the LDE is symmetric across gains and losses. Drawing on dual-process theories and prospect theory, the authors propose an analog value function that predicts the LDE should be more pronounced in loss contexts due to increased salience of value changes. Using a laboratory experiment and analysis of over 15 million real-world trades, the study tests this prediction. The key contribution is demonstrating that losses amplify the LDE—a previously unreported phenomenon—with implications for modeling financial behavior and designing interventions.

Academic research influences public opinion, but audiences rarely read full articles; instead, they rely on media summaries. The credibility of the researcher affects whether their findings are accepted. Prior research shows demographics like race and gender influence credibility, often favoring high-status groups. However, less is known about how individuals’ ideological beliefs—specifically egalitarianism or elitism—interact with these status cues. This paper addresses that gap by investigating how egalitarian and elitist ideologies shape credibility judgments of researchers based on their demographic status. Using status characteristic theory and social dominance orientation (SDO) as a measure of ideology, the authors propose a model in which ideology moderates the relationship between researcher status and credibility. They also test whether specific competence-related cues can override these ideologically driven biases. The key contribution is demonstrating that both egalitarian and elitist ideologies introduce directional bias in credibility evaluation, and that specific status cues can neutralize such bias.

Unemployment has major personal and societal costs, and while economic factors are important, psychological traits may also influence employment outcomes. Prior research on personality and unemployment has relied on measures taken after individuals entered the labor market, making it unclear whether personality affects unemployment or vice versa. This study addresses that gap by using pre-labor-market personality data from the British Cohort Study (N = 4,206) to test whether conscientiousness and other Big Five traits in adolescence predict unemployment over a 26-year period. The research question is whether higher conscientiousness at age 16–17 predicts lower unemployment from age 16 to 42. The study uses longitudinal regression and mediation analysis, controlling for intelligence, gender, and parental SES. The authors claim their findings clarify the direction of influence and show a meaningful effect of early personality on long-term employment.

title: 10.1016/j.obhdp.2015.01.004
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing workplace diversity, managers often assume consumers will react negatively to Black leaders, potentially limiting minority advancement. While prior research shows that racial stereotypes affect leader evaluations, it remains unclear whether such bias extends to consumer behavior toward the organization itself. This study addresses the gap by investigating whether and when leader race influences consumer purchasing behavior. Drawing on implicit leadership theory and motivated social cognition, the authors propose that negative reactions to Black leaders emerge primarily when organizational failure motivates stereotype application. Using archival data from professional sports, classroom experiments, and a controlled study, they test how performance, time, familiarity, and self-enhancement motives shape bias. The research contributes by showing that leader race affects consumer behavior not just through employee-customer interactions, but symbolically, as leaders represent their organizations.

Innovative behavior is critical for organizational success, yet it remains challenging to promote because employees may doubt whether their ideas will be valued or successfully implemented. While research has linked self-efficacy to creativity, less is known about how different types of self-efficacy influence distinct phases of innovation—generating, spreading, and implementing ideas—over time. Drawing on social–cognitive theory, this study addresses this gap by proposing a dynamic, moderated mediation model. It asks whether increases in organizational trust and perceived respect lead to increases in domain-specific self-efficacy (creative, persuasion, and change), which in turn promote different types of innovative behavior. Furthermore, it tests whether psychological collectivism, a between-individual trait, moderates these within-individual processes. Using longitudinal data from 267 Italian employees across three time points, the study applies latent growth modeling and regression analyses to examine change over an 8-month period. The authors claim a contribution by advancing an agentic perspective on innovation and demonstrating how socio-cognitive factors interact with individual differences to shape innovation dynamics.

Firms facing performance shortfalls below aspiration levels are theorized to engage in strategic actions, but prior research largely focuses on market-based responses like R&D. This study addresses a gap by asking whether firms also respond through nonmarket actions—specifically corporate lobbying—and whether the timing of these actions differs based on risk preferences. It proposes that risk-averse responses drive immediate lobbying increases, while risk-taking drives longer-term R&D investments. The authors use a behavioral theory of the firm (BTOF) framework, combined with firm-level panel data across 27 years. Their key claimed contribution is demonstrating a timing differential in strategic responses to performance gaps, integrating nonmarket behavior into the BTOF.

Multi-party collaborations are common in inter-firm alliances, yet most research has focused on dyadic relationships, leaving the formation of groups with three or more firms underexplored. While dyadic studies emphasize prior ties and homophily, it remains unclear how group-level constructs influence multi-party collaboration formation. This paper addresses this gap by studying VC syndicates—where 44-60% of deals involve three or more firms—focusing on how prior tie density affects syndicate formation. Using a sample of 1,336 real and 6,680 hypothetical U.S. syndicates from 1985–2008, the authors analyze formation as a group-level process. They find that tie density has a stronger positive effect when syndicates are larger, when status heterogeneity or subgroups exist, and when industries are more popular, contributing to network and VC literature by showing that multi-party formation is not simply an extension of dyadic logic.

Middle managers are critical for strategy implementation, and their voluntary turnover can disrupt organizational effectiveness. While research shows that leader humility reduces subordinate turnover by increasing job satisfaction, this effect may depend on contextual factors. Existing studies largely ignore how the broader leadership context—specifically the dynamics within the top management team (TMT)—can shape these micro-level leadership effects. This study addresses that gap by asking whether TMT faultlines, which create subgroup divisions within the TMT, limit the retention benefits of humble leadership. Using a multisource dataset of 43 TMTs and 502 middle managers, the authors test a multilevel model in which TMT faultlines moderate both the relationship between executive humility and middle manager job satisfaction, and the relationship between job satisfaction and voluntary turnover. The study contributes by identifying a cross-level boundary condition for leader humility and showing how macro-level team dynamics can undermine micro-level retention processes.

Although positive safety climate is generally linked to better safety outcomes, it may not always reduce risk, particularly in contexts where workers are detached from the consequences of their decisions—such as in engineering design. In such settings, production pressures like deadlines may shift priorities away from safety. This study investigates whether working to deadlines moderates the relationship between positive team safety climate and safety risk, as indicated by heuristic use at the individual level and design complexity at the team level. Using experience sampling and multilevel modeling, the authors test if safety climate has opposing effects depending on deadline pressure. The contribution lies in challenging the assumption that positive safety climate is universally beneficial by identifying boundary conditions under which it may increase risk.

Underemployment is widespread and often assumed to lead to negative employee outcomes. However, this paper challenges that view by investigating how underemployed employees might engage in positive behaviors like creativity and organizational citizenship behavior (OCBO). The authors identify a key gap: prior research has overlooked active coping strategies employees may use, such as task crafting. Drawing on the job crafting perspective, they propose a serial curvilinear mediated moderation model in which task crafting explains the link between underemployment and these positive outcomes. They test whether the relationship between perceived underemployment and task crafting is inverted U-shaped and moderated by organizational identification. The contribution is showing that underemployment can lead to beneficial outcomes under certain conditions, shifting the narrative from purely negative reactions.

title: 10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.07.004
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

entries.rq_with_context: Monitoring failures—where regulators or auditors fail to detect or report infractions—are a persistent problem in economic and regulatory systems. While weak relationships are often blamed for such failures due to poor coordination and mistrust, research on organizational deviance suggests that strong, trusting relationships may encourage negligence, bias, and collusion. This creates a theoretical tension: relationship strength may both help and harm monitoring quality. The paper addresses this gap by proposing a U-shaped relationship between relationship strength and monitoring failures. The research question is whether moderate-strength relationships yield the highest monitoring quality, with failures rising at both low and high levels of relational strength. The study uses a multi-method approach—archival data on financial restatements, a survey of CPAs, and an experimental audit simulation—to test this hypothesis. The key contribution claimed is the identification of a curvilinear effect of relationship strength on monitoring quality, reconciling conflicting perspectives in organizational theory.

Despite growing interest in alliance portfolios, the performance consequences of alliance portfolio diversity (APD) remain theoretically unclear and empirically inconsistent. While some studies suggest diversity brings benefits such as greater innovativeness and resource access, others highlight costs like coordination complexity and reduced trust. This lack of consensus calls for a systematic synthesis of existing findings. Using meta-analysis, the study investigates the overall effect of APD on performance and probes how this relationship is influenced by contextual factors such as level of analysis, performance measure, diversity domain, and diversity type. It further examines how researchers' theoretical orientations—transaction-cost economics (TCE), resource-based view (RBV), knowledge and learning, and social network theory—shape reported results. The study aims to clarify conflicting findings by uncovering patterns tied to theoretical and operational choices, offering guidance for more coherent future research.

Women remain underrepresented in top management despite organizational efforts and diversity initiatives. Existing explanations often focus on women’s career choices or lack of ambition, encouraging them to 'lean in.' However, these accounts typically treat career decisions as independent of prior experiences with employers, especially rejection in recruitment processes. This paper addresses the gap by exploring how past recruitment rejections—particularly women’s status as a negatively stereotyped minority—shape their decisions about future opportunities. The research asks whether and why women are less likely than men to consider jobs at firms that have previously rejected them. The authors use a theoretical framework combining motivational theories of procedural justice and belonging uncertainty, tested across three studies: archival data from an executive search firm, a survey of executives, and an experiment. The key contribution is identifying a supply-side mechanism—gender-differentiated responses to rejection—that interacts with demand-side discrimination to perpetuate gender inequality at the top of organizations.

The phenomenon under study is the relationship between team tenure and team psychological safety climate, a construct reflecting shared perceptions of interpersonal risk-taking safety. Despite theoretical expectations of a linear positive relationship, empirical findings have been mixed, suggesting a more complex pattern. This study addresses the gap by applying group formation theories, which suggest that both new and long-tenured teams experience higher psychological safety than moderate-tenure teams due to initial positive assumptions and later developed trust, respectively. The research question is whether team tenure has a curvilinear (U-shaped) relationship with team psychological safety climate and climate strength, and whether these in turn influence average team member creative and task performance. The study uses a multilevel structural equation model with data from 115 R&D teams in China. The key claimed contribution is demonstrating that team tenure’s effect on psychological safety and performance is nonlinear, and that climate strength plays a conditional role in performance outcomes.

Organizational ambidexterity—the ability to balance exploration and exploitation—is critical for firm performance, especially in dynamic environments. While prior research links TMT processes to ambidexterity, less is known about the boundary conditions, particularly how environmental dynamism affects this relationship. This study addresses that gap by focusing on small-sized SBUs where structural separation between exploration and exploitation is often impractical. Drawing on upper echelon theory and team processes research, it investigates how TMT behavioral integration fosters ambidexterity, and whether this effect is stronger under high environmental dynamism. The authors use data from 101 SBUs to test their hypotheses, contributing empirical evidence on when and how TMTs enable ambidextrous orientations in smaller, autonomous units.

Supervisors with a bottom-line mentality (BLM) prioritize financial outcomes over employee well-being and ethical concerns, potentially harming workplace relationships. While prior research links supervisor BLM to negative behaviors like coworker undermining and unethical conduct, it does not fully explain how employees perceive these supervisors or why they respond negatively. This study addresses that gap by investigating how supervisor BLM influences employee perceptions of LMX and subsequent task performance. Drawing on social exchange theory, the authors propose that high-BLM supervisors are seen as low-quality exchange partners, leading employees to withhold performance in return. The model is tested using two time-lagged, multi-source field studies (N = 189 and N = 244), with LMX as a mediator and employee BLM as a moderator. The main contribution is identifying a counterproductive cycle: supervisors focused on the bottom line ironically undermine the very performance they seek.

Charismatic leadership is an attribution made by followers based on perceived inspirational qualities, and prior research emphasizes the role of leader affective displays in shaping these perceptions. However, little is known about the antecedents of these affective processes, particularly how basic physiological factors like sleep influence them. This paper addresses this gap by examining whether leader and follower sleep deprivation—through their impact on emotional regulation and experience—harm attributions of charismatic leadership. Drawing from the emotional labor model of leadership and the sleep and affect regulation model, the authors test these effects using two laboratory experiments: one manipulating leader sleep and the other manipulating follower sleep. The study contributes by identifying sleep as a foundational antecedent of charismatic leadership, showing how both leader and follower states matter for leadership perceptions.

Short-term bonuses are widely used to motivate employees, yet there is limited empirical evidence on their effectiveness, particularly regarding different bonus types and their long-term impact on performance. While existing research supports the incentive effect of performance-based rewards, theories like cognitive evaluation theory suggest that extrinsic rewards may undermine intrinsic motivation, especially when they are small or perceived as controlling. This study addresses this gap by testing how cash, nonmonetary (pizza voucher), and verbal rewards influence productivity in a real workplace. Using a field experiment in a semiconductor factory, the authors compare productivity during and after bonus administration across four conditions. They find that all bonuses increase performance initially, but only monetary bonuses lead to a drop in productivity afterward. The key contribution is demonstrating that the form and delivery of short-term bonuses—especially whether employees choose them—affect both immediate performance and post-bonus motivation.

title: 10.1016/j.obhdp.2014.10.005
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

entries.rq_with_context: Emotions in negotiation have been studied primarily in distributive settings, focusing on simple emotional expressions like anger or happiness. Less is known about how complex emotions—such as emotional ambivalence, involving mixed positive and negative feelings—affect outcomes in integrative negotiations where value creation is possible. Prior research suggests that expressing ambivalence is detrimental in zero-sum contexts because it signals submissiveness and invites dominance. However, this may change in cooperative, integrative settings where assertiveness is necessary to achieve joint gains. This paper investigates whether expressed emotional ambivalence can improve integrative outcomes by triggering assertive responses through perceived submissiveness. The authors test this through three experiments using standardized negotiation tasks. Their contribution is to demonstrate that ambivalence, typically seen as a liability, can in fact be beneficial in cooperative negotiations by unlocking integrative potential.

Many organizational fields experience a resurgence of traditional arrangements despite processes of modernization, yet we lack understanding of how decomposed institutional logics reemerge to drive field-level change. While prior research acknowledges that logics leave behind traces after decomposition, it does not explain how these institutional remnants facilitate regeneration over time. This study investigates how the traditional craft-brewing logic reemerged in the Dutch beer industry after nearly disappearing due to industrialization. Drawing on an in-depth, historically embedded qualitative analysis, the authors trace the process through which networks of actors rediscovered, repurposed, and reused remnants of craft brewing. The approach follows a process research and grounded theory methodology, identifying three stages of regenerative change. The study contributes by developing a theory of regenerative institutional change through logic reemergence, highlighting the dualistic nature of restoration and transformation in such processes.

Despite decades of motivation research, the field continues to treat motivation as a matter of finding the right 'levers' to pull—be they rewards, goals, or discursive narratives. In response, scholars have taken a 'turn to identity,' exploring how employees construct desirable selves through work. However, this approach still assumes motivation can be engineered through organizational discourses. The paper critiques this by asking how motivation functions at the intersection of identity work when viewed through unconscious dynamics. Drawing on Lacanian psychoanalysis and 51 employee narratives, it explores how motivation discourse is used not only to construct idealized, 'imaginary' selves but also to unsettle and work through these fantasies. The study uses a narrative, Lacanian-informed analysis to show that motivation involves an ongoing internal struggle between desires for fulfillment and the structural impossibility of satisfaction at work. Its contribution lies in revealing how motivation can be an empowering process of articulating desire, rather than a tool for organizational control.

Research on multimarket contact and firm performance has produced mixed results, with some studies showing positive effects, others negative or no effects. This inconsistency remains unexplained despite theoretical advances. To address this gap, the authors propose that the relationship between multimarket contact and firm performance is curvilinear—specifically, inverted U-shaped—such that moderate levels of contact enhance performance through mutual forbearance, while low or high levels do not. They further argue that strategic alliances moderate this relationship by enhancing a firm’s ability to deter rivals. Using a sample of 233 semiconductor firms across 52 markets, they test these hypotheses with longitudinal data. The study contributes by clarifying the non-linear nature of multimarket contact effects and introducing strategic alliances as a key contingency.

Organizational citizenship behaviors (OCBs) are vital for organizational effectiveness, yet existing research on organizational climate and OCBs typically uses a variable-centered approach that isolates climate dimensions. This study responds to calls for more holistic, configurational views of climate by examining how combinations of values—based on the competing values framework (CVF)—form a constructive organizational values climate. The gap lies in understanding how these configurations, rather than individual dimensions, influence OCBs. The research asks how such a climate configuration relates to helping, taking charge, and creative behaviors, using a mesolevel climate perspective that bridges macro-level values and micro-level employee behaviors. It proposes and tests a model where affective commitment and psychological empowerment mediate these relationships, drawing on regulatory focus theory to explain distinct pathways for affiliative and change-oriented OCBs.

Trust is critical for small group functioning, yet how it develops in new groups remains unclear. While prior research shows that mean levels of trust or shared low trust affect group outcomes, little is known about the impact of diversity in initial trust tendencies—propensity to trust—among members. This gap is important because group members often differ in how readily they trust others, and such differences could disrupt trust formation regardless of overall trust levels. The authors propose that diversity in propensity to trust leads to frustration and perceptions of low similarity, reducing early intragroup trust, increasing relationship conflict, further eroding trust, and ultimately impairing performance. Using a longitudinal study of MBA student groups, they test this spiral model. The contribution is identifying diversity in a deep-level trait as a sufficient trigger for downward trust spirals, independent of mean trust levels.

Exit is a critical yet underexplored part of the entrepreneurial process, especially when founders leave successful ventures. While research acknowledges that founders often identify strongly with their organizations—sometimes viewing them as 'children'—there is limited understanding of how they psychologically disengage during voluntary exits. The existing literature tends to frame exit as failure or focuses on strategic decisions, neglecting the personal, emotional, and identity-related aspects. This study addresses this gap by investigating how founders manage psychological disengagement during voluntary exits from successful ventures and how this influences their transition to new ventures. Through a qualitative, inductive study of technology founders, the author develops a theoretical model linking work orientations to disengagement paths. The contribution lies in explaining how internal motivations shape disengagement tactics, identification dynamics, and emotional experiences.

The phenomenon under study is the challenge scholars face when transferring research from base disciplines (e.g., psychology, sociology) to interdisciplinary management journals like AMJ. There is a gap in understanding how AMJ’s expectations for theoretical contribution, theory development, and methodological rigor differ from those in discipline-specific journals, which can lead to misaligned submissions. The research question is: How do AMJ’s disciplinary norms diverge from those in base-discipline journals, and what adjustments should authors make when targeting AMJ? The authors use their editorial experience and observational analysis to outline key differences across three areas: contribution (the 'porridge'), theory development (the 'chair'), and method (the 'bed'). Their claimed contribution is practical guidance that clarifies AMJ’s implicit standards to help base-discipline scholars successfully navigate the publication process.

Foreign firms often struggle to build political capital in host countries due to the liability of foreignness, which limits their access to political and regulatory players. While political capital is known to influence firm outcomes, less is understood about how disadvantaged firms can effectively acquire it. This study addresses that gap by investigating whether foreign-owned defense contractors can leverage outside lobbyists to improve their chances of winning U.S. defense contracts. Drawing on certification theory, the paper argues that outside lobbyists serve as credible intermediaries who certify foreign firms and facilitate information flow. Using data on U.S. Department of Defense contracts from 1998 to 2006, the study analyzes lobbying expenditures and contract outcomes. It contributes by showing how external political strategies can offset disadvantages in political embeddedness.

There is a well-documented divide between academic management research and its practical usefulness for organizations, with much of the research being irrelevant to real-world business challenges. Existing approaches often fail to engage organizational stakeholders in the research process, limiting access to data and reducing the applicability of findings. This paper asks how action research can be used to bridge this theory-practice gap by producing both scientific and practical value. It explores the process, benefits, and implementation of action research from the perspectives of researchers, organizations, and academic institutions. The approach is grounded in a definition of action research as a collaborative process aimed at generating actionable knowledge. The authors claim the contribution is a practical primer that clarifies how action research works and why it benefits all parties involved.

Employees differ in how much they value extrinsic rewards like money and recognition at work, yet performance management practices like competence feedback are often applied uniformly without considering such individual differences. While competence supportive feedback is generally shown to enhance performance and well-being, it remains unclear for whom and under what conditions these benefits hold. This study investigates whether extrinsic value orientation (EVO) moderates the effects of competence feedback on in-role and extra-role performance, and on subjective well-being. Drawing on self-determination theory and trait activation theory, the research uses two employee samples to test interactive effects. The key contribution is identifying that EVO strengthens feedback’s positive impact on performance but weakens its benefits for well-being, with experienced work demands as an underlying mechanism.

The global platform economy enables individuals from emerging economies—many from countries not traditionally associated with offshoring—to work directly for international clients.
