When goal competitiveness is low, abuse triggers empathic emotion and increases helping; when high, it triggers schadenfreude and reduces helping. The research uses one experiment and one field study to test this moderated mediation model. The contribution lies in challenging the assumption of uniform observer alignment with victims and identifying a key boundary condition that explains divergent emotional and behavioral responses.

title: Empathy or schadenfreude? Exploring observers’ differential responses to abusive supervision

entries.rq_with_context: Compassion in organizations has been linked to better well-being, engagement, and performance, yet little research has explored how to foster it beyond meditation-based interventions. Most existing studies focus on employees rather than managers, despite the critical role managers play in modeling compassionate behavior. This study addresses these gaps by testing a new emotional skills cultivation training (ESCT) among managers. The research question is whether improving emotional skills—such as awareness, understanding, and management of emotions—can enhance managers’ sense of compassion, reduce fear of compassion, and improve follower-rated outcomes like servant leadership and autonomy support. Using a quasi-randomized controlled trial with pre- and post-tests, the study measures both self-rated and follower-rated changes. The contribution lies in demonstrating a non-meditation-based intervention that targets compassion through emotional skills training in managerial roles.

title: Awakening Compassion in Managers—a New Emotional Skills Intervention to Improve Managerial Compassion

entries.rq_with_context: Research has shown that employee authenticity is linked to positive work outcomes, but the underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions remain unclear. Most studies are cross-sectional and lack insight into how authenticity translates into employee well-being and performance. This study addresses these gaps by testing whether psychological capital (PsyCap) mediates the relationship between employee authenticity and work attitudes/behaviors, using a three-wave survey of 588 employees in China. It also examines whether leader authenticity moderates the strength of this mediation. The study draws on the job demands-resources (JD-R) model and conservation of resources (COR) theory. Its contribution lies in identifying PsyCap as a key mechanism and leader authenticity as a contextual enhancer.

title: How Employee Authenticity Shapes Work Attitudes and Behaviors: the Mediating Role of Psychological Capital and the Moderating Role of Leader Authenticity

entries.rq_with_context: Despite widespread use of control variables in organizational and social science research, their inclusion is often automatic and theoretically unjustified, leading to potentially flawed inferences. Existing literature highlights the risks of misusing controls but offers limited guidance on how to systematically evaluate alternative explanations for observed relationships. This paper addresses that gap by proposing the Hierarchical Iterative Control (HIC) approach, which involves testing whether control variables account for observed X-Y relationships through a structured sequence of empirical tests. The research question is how researchers can use control variables more effectively to rule in or out plausible mechanisms—such as common method variance or confounding constructs—that might explain why variables are related. The approach is grounded in a programmatic, theory-driven strategy involving multiple studies and methods. The key contribution is a 7-step framework that shifts control variables from statistical afterthoughts to central tools for building evidence about causal mechanisms.

title: Mastering the Use of Control Variables: the Hierarchical Iterative Control (HIC) Approach

entries.rq_with_context: Automation in management, particularly using AI and machine learning, is increasingly common, yet little is known about how it changes managerial work beyond efficiency and effectiveness. While prior research focuses on whether automation improves decision outcomes or whether people trust algorithmic recommendations, this study addresses a gap by exploring how the implementation of automated systems affects managers' psychological experiences during work. Drawing on work design theory, the authors examine how the timing of automated support—before or after human information processing—influences task performance, time to decide, enjoyment, satisfaction, and self-efficacy in personnel selection. Using a lab experiment with 122 participants across three conditions, the study tests these effects in a controlled setting. The key claimed contribution is advancing understanding of how automation shapes work characteristics and psychological outcomes in management, thereby encouraging research on automation’s broader impact on job satisfaction and well-being.

title: Changing the means of managerial work: effects of automated decision support systems on personnel selection tasks

entries.rq_with_context: While existing research treats social stressors (e.g., conflicts, injustice) as uniformly harmful, this paper challenges that view by introducing 'social challenge stressors'—socially tense situations inherent to task accomplishment that require effortful social coordination. Although the challenge-hindrance stressor framework has been applied to non-social job demands, it has not been extended to social aspects of work. This study fills that gap by developing a new scale for social challenge stressors and testing their dual impact on well-being and strain. Using multiple samples, including a longitudinal design, the authors examine whether these stressors uniquely predict both positive (e.g., self-esteem, efficacy) and negative (e.g., emotional exhaustion) outcomes, even after controlling for established social stressors. The approach integrates the challenge-hindrance framework with the stress-as-offense-to-self model, focusing on self-esteem as a key mechanism. The study contributes a novel construct and measurement tool, offering a more nuanced understanding of how social job demands can be both taxing and beneficial.

title: Social Job Stressors can Foster Employee Well-Being: Introducing the Concept of Social Challenge Stressors

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses a popular claim—widely discussed in The New York Times and The Washington Post—that women perform more office housework (OHW), suffer more burnout, and receive fewer career benefits than men for such work. However, this claim has not been formally tested. The research gap lies in the lack of scholarly definition, measurement, and empirical investigation of OHW as a distinct construct, particularly its differential implications by gender. The study tests whether gender differences in OHW exist, whether OHW contributes to burnout, and whether the career payoff from OHW differs by gender. Using gender role theory, conservation of resources theory, and shifting standards, the authors test their hypotheses with three-wave survey data from U.S. employees. The study's contribution is twofold: it introduces and validates OHW as a measurable construct and empirically examines a widely cited but untested claim about gender, work, and career outcomes.

title: Office Housework, Burnout, and Promotion: Does Gender Matter?

entries.rq_with_context: Research has shown that insufficient effort responding (IER) can confound survey measures by inflating observed correlations, particularly when attentive respondents' scores deviate from the scale midpoint. However, it remains unclear whether IER similarly affects objective tests and their relationships with survey measures. Additionally, while simulation studies have explored IER's impact, two key parameters—within-person consistency of IER and the percentage of IER in a sample—have not been systematically examined. This study addresses these gaps using empirical data from a training study (Study 1) and a follow-up simulation (Study 2). The research asks: (1) Is IER negatively related to performance on objective tests and does it change the correlation between surveys and tests? (2) How do within-person consistency and prevalence of IER jointly influence the magnitude of confounding? The approach combines observational analysis with bootstrapped simulations to model varying levels of IER. The authors claim their work advances understanding of when and how IER biases findings across measurement methods.

title: Insufficient Effort Responding as a Potential Confound between Survey Measures and Objective Tests

entries.rq_with_context: Deceptive impression management (IM), such as exaggerating or fabricating experiences during job interviews, remains a persistent challenge in personnel selection. While prior research has identified personality and situational predictors of faking, less is known about the proximal psychological mechanisms—particularly emotional states like anxiety—that drive such behavior. This paper addresses this gap by investigating whether interview anxiety, rooted in concerns about self-presentation, is linked to deceptive IM. Drawing on Schlenker and Leary’s (1982) theory that social anxiety stems from self-presentational concerns, the authors propose that anxiety may motivate applicants to manage impressions deceptively to protect self-esteem or secure rewards. Using survey data from applicants after real job interviews, the study tests three hypotheses: (1) interview anxiety positively relates to deceptive IM, (2) honesty-humility indirectly reduces deceptive IM via lower anxiety, and (3) extraversion indirectly reduces deceptive IM through reduced anxiety. The contribution lies in being the first to empirically link interview anxiety to deceptive IM and position it as a mediating mechanism between personality and faking.

title: Shake and Fake: the Role of Interview Anxiety in Deceptive Impression Management

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace incivility is common and harmful, yet organizations rely on reference checks to screen out uncivil applicants—assuming that people are unwilling to recommend rude colleagues. However, little research has tested this assumption. This paper investigates whether perceived colleague incivility affects willingness to recommend, and whether factors like job performance or job-level characteristics weaken this effect. Using signaling theory, the authors test these relationships across two studies: one examining boundary conditions and another testing an organizational intervention. The research contributes by revealing when incivility is overlooked in recommendations and how organizations can strengthen its impact during hiring.

title: Willingness to Recommend: Does Workplace Incivility Actually Play a Role?

entries.rq_with_context: Proactive personality has been linked to creative behavior, but the mechanisms behind this relationship remain unclear. While prior research suggests proactive individuals are more creative, less is known about the psychological processes that translate this trait into creative outcomes. This study addresses this gap by proposing that thriving at work—characterized by vitality and learning—mediates the relationship between proactive personality and creative behavior. Drawing on trait activation theory, the study also examines whether high-involvement HR practices (e.g., autonomy, information sharing, training) enhance the tendency of proactive employees to thrive. The analysis uses survey data from employees and supervisors in China, tested via structural equation modeling. The study contributes by identifying a key mediating mechanism and an important contextual moderator.

title: Proactive Personality and Creative Behavior: Examining the Role of Thriving at Work and High-Involvement HR Practices

entries.rq_with_context: Despite theoretical and empirical support for a positive link between learning goal orientation (LGO) and performance, findings have been inconsistent, with some studies showing null or negative effects. This suggests the need to identify boundary conditions. The authors propose task variety—the extent to which a job involves diverse tasks—as a key moderator. Drawing on trait activation theory and attention capacity theory, they argue that high task variety may both activate LGO and deplete cognitive resources. Using multi-source data from 155 employees in South Korean firms, they test whether task variety moderates the LGO–performance relationship. Their main contribution is identifying task variety as a situational factor that shapes when LGO enhances or undermines performance.

title: Effect of Learning Goal Orientation on Performance: Role of Task Variety as a Moderator

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace incivility is common and often witnessed by bystanders, yet not all choose to intervene. Existing research has examined factors influencing third-party intervention, but less is known about how multiple situational cues combine to shape decisions, particularly when ambiguity and cost-reward considerations compete. This study integrates Latané and Darley’s decision-tree model and Piliavin et al.’s arousal: cost-reward model to test how ambiguity-reduction and cost-reward cues jointly influence bystander intervention. It further investigates whether moral identity, observer role, and perpetrator-target gender composition moderate these effects. Using policy capturing with over 3,400 participants, the authors examine the relative weight of these cues in shaping two forms of prosocial intervention: supporting the target and confronting the perpetrator. The study contributes by identifying which cues matter most, for whom, and under what conditions, advancing a more integrated understanding of bystander decision-making in response to low-intensity mistreatment.

title: A Policy Capturing Investigation of Bystander Decisions to Intervene against Workplace Incivility

entries.rq_with_context: People belong to multiple social groups simultaneously, yet most stereotype research focuses on single categories like race or gender. This study addresses the gap by exploring how intersecting identities—such as ethnicity, gender, age, and sexual orientation—affect fundamental dimensions of social perception: warmth and competence. Existing models like double jeopardy predict worsening stigma with more minority identities, but little empirical work tests these ideas using warmth/competence frameworks. The current research asks how professional workers perceive various combinations of these four demographic categories in workplace contexts. Using the Stereotype Content Model (SCM), the study analyzes ratings from recruiters and employees. It contributes initial evidence on intersectional stereotypes, showing that multiple-group memberships do not always compound disadvantage and may even offset negative perceptions.

title: Multiple-group membership: warmth and competence perceptions in the workplace

entries.rq_with_context: Despite technological advances, videoconference interviews still result in lower performance ratings and more negative applicant perceptions compared to face-to-face interviews, though the reasons remain unclear. Previous research has identified potential factors like impaired non-verbal communication and reduced social presence, but few studies have experimentally tested these mechanisms using current technology. This study addresses this gap by comparing the two formats in a simulated selection setting, focusing on performance ratings and applicant perceptions. The research question is: which factors—specifically social presence, eye contact, and impression management—account for differences in interview outcomes between face-to-face and videoconference interviews? The study uses experimental design with mediation analysis based on social presence theory and media attributes framework. It contributes by identifying specific psychological mechanisms that explain performance differences and applicant reactions.

title: It Takes More Than a Good Camera: Which Factors Contribute to Differences Between Face-to-Face Interviews and Videoconference Interviews Regarding Performance Ratings and Interviewee Perceptions?

entries.rq_with_context: Although laissez-faire leadership is known to have negative effects on employee outcomes, less is known about the underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions that explain when and why these effects occur. Existing research has largely overlooked how individual differences might shape employee responses to passive leadership styles. This study addresses this gap by investigating the role of subordinate relational self-concept—a disposition emphasizing dyadic relationships—as a moderator in the relationship between laissez-faire leadership and affective organizational commitment (AOC). Drawing on social exchange theory and the identity orientation framework, the authors propose that employees with strong relational self-concepts will react more negatively to laissez-faire leadership because it violates their expectations for relational engagement. The research uses a three-wave longitudinal design with structural equation modeling and full information maximum likelihood estimation on a sample of 449 employees to test a moderated mediation model. The key contribution is identifying both a specific mechanism (LMX contribution) and a personal boundary condition (relational self-concept) that clarify the contingent impact of laissez-faire leadership.

title: Laissez-Faire Leadership and Affective Commitment: the Roles of Leader-Member Exchange and Subordinate Relational Self-concept

entries.rq_with_context: Management and applied psychology face concerns about questionable research practices like p-hacking and HARKing, which undermine research credibility. Although preregistration is promoted as a solution to increase transparency, its actual effectiveness and researchers’ perceptions of it remain understudied in this field. This paper investigates whether preregistered studies display more transparent reporting practices—such as stating sample size rationales and having a priori analysis plans—compared to non-preregistered studies. Using a mixed-methods approach, Study 1 compares published preregistered and non-preregistered samples, while Study 2 surveys researchers with and without preregistration experience. The study finds that preregistration is associated with more transparent reporting and fewer significant results, and reveals that while researchers are generally supportive, they express concerns about time, flexibility, and being scooped. The contribution is empirical evidence and stakeholder-informed insights on preregistration's real and perceived value.

title: Study Preregistration: An Evaluation of a Method for Transparent Reporting

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly rely on teamwork, making peer ratings a common tool for assessing individual performance. However, it is unclear whether such ratings reflect the target’s actual behavior or are influenced by the team context. Existing research shows team-level variance in ratings but lacks theoretical explanation for its sources. This study addresses the gap by testing two theoretical explanations—situation strength (team influences behavior) versus social cognition (team influences perceiver judgments). Using cross-classified and social relations modeling, the authors examine whether team membership accounts for more perceiver or target variance in peer ratings. They also test psychological safety as a driver of perceiver-level variance. The key contribution is demonstrating that team context shapes how peers evaluate others more than it shapes individual behavior, challenging assumptions about the comparability of peer ratings across teams.

title: The Effects of Team Context on Peer Ratings of Task and Citizenship Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Disparities in occupational attainment between Black and White Americans are well documented, with race influencing access to higher-status jobs. Vocational interests are a key factor shaping career choices and outcomes, yet little is known about racial differences in these interests. Existing research suggests patterns but lacks a comprehensive, meta-analytic examination of Black-White differences across the full RIASEC framework. This study fills that gap by conducting a meta-analysis of 54 studies to determine the magnitude and direction of racial differences in vocational interests. Drawing on social identity theory and Gottfredson’s theory of circumscription and compromise, the authors examine how perceived accessibility of occupations may shape interest development. The study also investigates boundary conditions such as education level, age, birth cohort, and gender, offering insight into when and for whom these differences emerge.

title: Black-White differences in vocational interests: Meta-analysis and boundary conditions

entries.rq_with_context: Proactive behavior—self-initiated actions aimed at improving future outcomes—is increasingly valued in modern organizations. However, such behaviors may be evaluated differently depending on who performs them due to stereotypes linked to visible characteristics like age and gender. While prior research has examined single characteristics, little is known about how these factors interact, especially when combined with perceived motives. This paper addresses this gap by testing how the intersectionality of age, gender, and ascribed motives shapes effectiveness ratings of identical proactive behaviors. Using an experimental vignette design across two studies, the authors test specific hypotheses about when certain combinations (e.g., older men with achievement motives) receive higher ratings. The key contribution is demonstrating that evaluations depend not on isolated traits but on their combined configuration, advancing understanding of bias in performance assessments.

title: Making Things Happen (Un)Expectedly: Interactive Effects of Age, Gender, and Motives on Evaluations of Proactive Behavior

entries.rq_with_context: Team creativity is critical for organizational success, yet the collective mechanisms through which leadership influences it remain poorly understood. While transformational leadership is known to enhance creativity, the role of transactional leadership is less clear, and prior research has focused on interpersonal processes like communication rather than motivational mechanisms. This study addresses this gap by investigating two emergent team states—collective regulatory focus (CRF) and team initiative—as mediators linking leadership to team creativity. It also considers how team members’ chronic regulatory focus contributes to CRF emergence. Using an experimental team study and a survey, the authors test a moderated-mediation model. The key contribution is identifying CRF as a collective motivational mechanism that explains how leadership shapes team creativity beyond individual-level processes.

title: Collective aspirations: collective regulatory focus as a mediator between transformational and transactional leadership and team creativity

entries.rq_with_context: Job insecurity is a widespread issue in today’s volatile labor markets and has been shown to undermine employee well-being and performance. While prior research establishes that job insecurity reduces work engagement, which in turn harms job performance, less is known about the boundary conditions that might weaken this negative pathway. This study addresses that gap by exploring whether employees’ helping behaviors and prosocial motivation can buffer the adverse effects of job insecurity. Drawing on the job demands-resources (JD-R) model, the authors propose that when employees give help driven by prosocial motivation, the negative impact of job insecurity on engagement and performance is reduced. The research tests these ideas using two cross-sectional studies in the South Korean service sector.

title: When do job-insecure employees keep performing well? The buffering roles of help and prosocial motivation in the relationship between job insecurity, work engagement, and job performance

entries.rq_with_context: Employees in safety-critical industries are expected to consistently follow safety policies, yet organizations often assume uniformity in safety climate perceptions without assessing actual agreement. While prior research has focused on predicting safety climate strength, less is known about how it influences individual-level outcomes like safety motivation—the key psychological antecedent to safe behavior. There is a gap in understanding how group-level disagreement (or strength) in safety climate shapes motivation, particularly within self-determination theory. This study fills that gap by testing whether safety climate strength moderates the link between individual safety climate perceptions and identified safety motivation using multilevel analyses in a healthcare sample. The approach uses a multilevel model to account for both individual and group effects. The authors claim their study contributes to the nomological network of safety climate, motivation, and behavior by clarifying when and how situational pressure influences motivation.

title: Should We Agree to Disagree? The Multilevel Moderated Relationship Between Safety Climate Strength And Individual Safety Motivation

entries.rq_with_context: Video-based situational judgment tests (SJTs) are increasingly used in employee selection, but concerns remain about how demographic cues in these assessments may affect test taker performance and reactions. While research on relational demography and identity contingency cues suggests that people respond differently to in-group versus out-group members, it is unclear how such dynamics play out in video-based assessments where actors’ race and gender are visible. Although some studies suggest that imagined interracial interactions may trigger anxiety or attentional demands, it is unknown whether this affects SJT performance. The current research fills this gap by testing whether racial similarity between test takers and interaction partners in video SJTs influences item performance and organizational fit perceptions. Using two experimental studies with manipulated racial and gender cues, the authors examine main and interactive effects of race and gender on performance and reactions. The study contributes to understanding how media richness in assessments may introduce systematic bias and affect fairness.

title: Performance on Video-Based Situational Judgment Test Items: Simulated Interracial Interactions

entries.rq_with_context: Emergent leadership in virtual teams is critical for team success, yet it remains unclear which factors—leadership traits (ascription) or task-related behaviors (achievement)—are more influential in different virtual work contexts. Prior research has examined these pathways in isolation and often treated virtuality as a simple dichotomy, leaving a gap in understanding how leadership emergence varies across the virtuality spectrum. This study addresses this by simultaneously examining the incremental and relative importance of achievement and ascription antecedents across low, medium, and high virtuality settings using two independent samples. It also explores whether other-rated personality traits are stronger predictors than self-ratings. The study uses multilevel modeling and dominance analysis to test these relationships, ultimately contributing to leadership emergence theory by clarifying when and how different antecedents shape leadership emergence in virtual environments.

title: Who Emerges into Virtual Team Leadership Roles? The Role of Achievement and Ascription Antecedents for Leadership Emergence Across the Virtuality Spectrum

entries.rq_with_context: Meta-analytic reviews are considered foundational for cumulative knowledge and evidence-based practice in organizational research, yet the robustness of their results is rarely assessed. Despite turnover being a central topic in management research with high organizational costs, concerns about statistical power, questionable research practices, and lack of replication raise doubts about the reliability of existing meta-analytic conclusions. This study investigates how sensitive turnover meta-analyses are to outliers and publication bias by reanalyzing 205 effect size distributions from seven published meta-analyses. Using a comprehensive sensitivity analysis approach, it evaluates both individual and combined impacts of these biases. The key contribution is providing empirical evidence on the extent to which our cumulative knowledge on turnover may be distorted, thereby informing both researchers and practitioners about the trustworthiness of current recommendations.

title: How robust is our cumulative knowledge on turnover?

entries.rq_with_context: Negative performance feedback is known to trigger negative affect, but prior research often treats this as a broad construct rather than examining specific emotions. This paper addresses the gap by focusing on sadness as a distinct emotional reaction to negative feedback, using the appraisal tendency framework (ATF) to explain how such feedback leads to sadness due to low certainty and motive inconsistency. The research question is whether sadness mediates the relationship between negative feedback and later task performance, and whether feedback self-efficacy and grit buffer this effect. The authors test a mediated moderation model using experimental data with facial expression analysis. Their key contribution is identifying sadness as a critical mechanism in feedback processes and showing how personal traits can mitigate its spillover effects on performance.

title: Examining the effects of negative performance feedback: the roles of sadness, feedback self-efficacy, and grit

entries.rq_with_context: Leader-member exchange (LMX) theory emphasizes the dyadic relationship between leaders and employees, yet most research relies on only one party's perspective. Despite low agreement between leader and member LMX ratings, prior studies often treat them as interchangeable or aggregate them, raising conceptual and methodological concerns. This study addresses this gap by testing whether alignment in leader and member perceptions of LMX explains employee outcomes beyond individual perceptions, and when misalignment occurs, whose perception is more influential. Using social exchange theory, the authors test their model on 206 employees across 35 groups using HLM and polynomial regression. They find that alignment enhances understanding of outcomes, and in misalignment, the leader’s perception better predicts innovative performance, though not affective commitment or turnover.

title: Two to Tango? Implications of Alignment and Misalignment in Leader and Follower Perceptions of LMX

entries.rq_with_context: Newcomer adjustment is critical for both individuals and organizations, and prior research highlights the role of proactive behaviors and organizational tactics in socialization. However, less attention has been paid to exchange-based behaviors like helping others as a pathway to adjustment. This study addresses this gap by exploring how newcomers’ helping behavior affects their adjustment and whether coworkers’ attributions of motives (prosocial vs. impression management) strengthen or weaken these effects. Drawing on social exchange and attribution theories, the authors propose a moderated mediation model where helping behavior influences distal outcomes (organizational commitment) through proximal outcomes (task mastery and social integration), moderated by coworker-attributed motives. The study uses time-lagged survey data from 114 newcomer-coworker dyads in a Chinese company. Its key contribution is demonstrating that helping behavior benefits adjustment, especially when coworkers perceive it as driven by prosocial motives.

title: Helping others makes me fit better: effects of helping behavior by newcomers and coworker-attributed motives on newcomers’ adjustment

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational research has traditionally viewed workplace gossip as harmful, but scholars from other disciplines highlight its functional roles in information sharing and social bonding. Despite this, little is known about how the mere perception of gossip prevalence—rather than direct involvement—affects employees broadly. This paper addresses that gap by investigating both the benefits and costs of perceived work-related gossip prevalence using social information processing theory. The central research question is whether such perceptions lead to higher job performance via increased performance pressure, and lower psychological well-being due to constant monitoring and lack of trust, with both effects amplified by negative gossip valence. The authors test this model across an experiment and two multi-wave field studies in the USA and China. Their key contribution is framing gossip as a 'mixed blessing' rather than purely dysfunctional.

title: Are You Gossiping About Me? The Costs and Benefits of High Workplace Gossip Prevalence

entries.rq_with_context: Employees may feel stuck in their jobs due to job embeddedness—being tied to their organization through links, fit, and sacrifice—but it remains unclear whether such employees are satisfied with their work. While prior research has focused on how embeddedness reduces turnover, less is known about its impact on employee well-being. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether job embeddedness leads to higher job satisfaction through job crafting, where employees proactively adjust their tasks and relationships. Using a two-phase survey of employees in southern China, the authors test a moderated mediation model. They find that job crafting mediates the positive relationship between embeddedness and satisfaction, and that this process depends on employees’ goal-striving orientations—specifically, it is stronger for those high in accomplishment striving and weaker for those high in communion striving.

title: Can Job-Embedded Employees Be Satisfied? The Role of Job Crafting and Goal-Striving Orientations

entries.rq_with_context: Employees may engage in deviant behaviors when they intend to leave their organization, but it remains unclear how job opportunities shape this relationship. While prior research suggests that turnover intentions and deviance co-occur due to shared causes like perceived inequity, recent studies propose that deviance can be part of a psychological detachment process. However, little is known about how individual and contextual factors influence whether such intentions lead to minor or serious deviance. This study addresses this gap by testing whether education and industry unemployment rates—two indicators of job opportunity—moderate the relationship between turnover intentions and both minor and serious deviance. Using survey data from 1179 Swiss employees linked to official unemployment statistics, the authors employ logistic regression to examine these interactions. They contribute by showing how macro-level and individual factors jointly shape different forms of workplace deviance.

title: Aiming to Leave and Aiming to Harm: the Role of Turnover Intentions and Job Opportunities for Minor and Serious Deviance

entries.rq_with_context: Employees frequently share negative emotions and stressful experiences at work, yet little research has examined how their perceptions of others’ responses in these interactions shape workplace outcomes. While sensemaking theory suggests that interpersonal cues from such exchanges help individuals interpret their organizational role and identity, most prior research has focused on crises rather than everyday emotional interactions. This paper addresses that gap by investigating how perceived listener reactions—viewed as critical social cues—shape employees’ sense of inclusion and organization-based self-esteem. Drawing on sensemaking theory, the authors propose that positive reactions affirm one’s value and belonging, fostering stronger commitment and lower turnover intentions, whereas negative reactions threaten identity and produce opposite effects. Two studies test this model, with the second examining the role of communion striving as a moderator. The research contributes by linking emotion-sharing interactions to identity-based processes and clarifying when and how these cues matter most.

title: Sensemaking and Negative Emotion Sharing: Perceived Listener Reactions as Interpersonal Cues Driving Workplace Outcomes

entries.rq_with_context: Research has established that individual moral disengagement leads to unethical and harmful behaviors at work. However, little is known about how aggregating morally disengaged individuals into teams affects team-level outcomes. This paper addresses this gap by exploring how team-level moral disengagement composition influences team performance through team processes like cooperation and interpersonal deviance. Using a time-lagged design with 94 student teams, the authors test a model grounded in moral disengagement theory and the input-process-output (IPO) framework. They find that team MD composition negatively affects performance primarily through reduced cooperation, but this effect weakens in teams with high collective extraversion. The study contributes by extending moral disengagement theory to team contexts and identifying a boundary condition.

title: The impact of team moral disengagement composition on team performance: the roles of team cooperation, team interpersonal deviance, and collective extraversion

entries.rq_with_context: Workers’ compensation costs are a major expense for employers, and while training and job redesign have mixed results in reducing claims, applicant screening via integrity tests may offer an alternative. Prior studies suggest integrity testing reduces claims, but methodological issues—such as confounding by employee tenure—limit confidence in these findings. Additionally, mechanisms linking integrity test scores to outcomes like injuries and malingering remain untested. This paper investigates whether pre-hire integrity testing reduces claim rates and costs (Study 1), and explores the psychological mechanisms—via safety motivation, compliance, and malingering—through which specific test subscales operate (Study 2). Using archival data and a three-wave survey, the research applies a model integrating safety performance theory and malingering research. The authors claim their work clarifies theoretical mechanisms, improves on prior methodology, and demonstrates high return on investment for organizations.

title: Reducing Injuries, Malingering, and Workers’ Compensation Costs by Implementing Overt Integrity Testing

entries.rq_with_context: Ideal point personality measures, which include intermediate trait-level items, are gaining attention for their potential to improve measurement accuracy over traditional dominance measures that use only positive and negative items. However, no research has examined how test-takers react to ideal point measures, despite the known impact of reactions on applicant behaviors and organizational outcomes. Existing studies suggest reactions vary by personality test format, but it is unknown whether the more complex structure of ideal point items affects perceptions. This study compares reactions to ideal point and dominance measures in both honest and simulated applicant conditions. Using a mixed-methods design, it tests whether measure type influences perceived difficulty and accuracy, and whether these factors mediate affective reactions—especially under impression management pressure. The key contribution is providing the first evidence on applicant reactions to ideal point measures, informing their viability in personnel selection.

title: Test-taker reactions to ideal point measures of personality

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing recognition of the benefits of gender diversity on corporate boards, progress in increasing female representation has been slow and uneven across countries. Prior research has largely focused on either organizational factors (e.g., CEO characteristics, board structure) or national institutional contexts as separate predictors of female board representation, but few have examined how these levels interact. This paper addresses this gap by proposing that national gender equality context moderates the influence of organizational leadership on female board representation. Drawing on implicit bias theory, agency theory, and institutional theory, the authors conduct a meta-analysis of 158 samples from 36 countries to test this moderation effect. The key contribution is identifying national gender equality as a boundary condition that shapes how internal organizational mechanisms translate into gender-diverse boards.

title: Women on Boards of Directors: A Meta-Analytic Examination of the Roles of Organizational Leadership and National Context for Gender Equality

entries.rq_with_context: Faking in job interviews is a well-known issue in personnel selection, typically explained by individual differences like personality or attitudes. However, prior research has largely ignored potential regional variations in faking tendencies within a single country. Drawing on socioecological psychology, this study investigates whether applicants from different U.S. metropolitan areas differ in their faking intentions and whether regional-level predictors—such as macro-psychological traits (e.g., average conscientiousness or competitive worldviews in a region)—explain these differences. The authors test both individual- and region-level predictors using multilevel modeling on data from 4,860 MTurk workers across the 50 largest U.S. metropolitan areas. They find that while individual traits matter, regional averages of conscientiousness and competitive worldviews also predict regional faking levels, with competitive worldviews showing a contextual effect beyond individual scores. The key contribution is demonstrating that faking intentions are not only shaped by individual traits but also by the psychological climate of the region.

title: Do You Fake More Because of Your Neighbors? A Multi-level Study on Regional and Individual Predictors of Faking Intentions Across the USA

entries.rq_with_context: Optimism has been widely studied for its positive effects on employee outcomes such as performance, engagement, and well-being. While prior research has examined employee and supervisor optimism separately, little is known about how their combined levels—specifically similarity or dissimilarity—affect subordinates. This study addresses this gap by investigating the impact of supervisor-subordinate optimism (dis)similarity on subordinates’ role conflict, vigor, and subsequent job performance. Drawing on expectancy-value theory, it proposes that mismatched optimism levels create conflicting role expectations, leading to role conflict. This stressor is expected to deplete subordinates' vigor and ultimately reduce performance. Polynomial regression and response surface analysis were used with a sample of 556 subordinates and 151 supervisors. The study contributes by showing that supervisor optimism is not universally beneficial and may harm less optimistic subordinates when dissimilar.

title: Leader-Follower (Dis) Similarity in Optimism: Its Effect on Followers’ Role Conflict, Vigor and Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Distributive justice research has long focused on the fairness of resource allocation, yet little attention has been paid to how the type of resource being distributed affects employee reactions. While equity theory suggests that people may respond differently depending on the nature of the exchanged resource, most studies either fail to specify the resource focus or aggregate across multiple resources. This lack of specificity creates a gap in understanding which resources matter most when assessing justice perceptions. The authors address this by asking whether distributive justice effects differ systematically across resource foci and whether individual differences in personal valence moderate these effects. Using a meta-analysis of existing studies and a policy capturing study with five specific resources (pay, work schedule flexibility, recognition, interesting work assignments, developmental opportunities), they examine both cross-resource and individual-level variations. Their key contribution is clarifying that while prior literature shows comparable effects across unspecified resources, more controlled analysis reveals pay-related justice has stronger impacts, and personal valence significantly shapes reactions.

title: Distributive Justice: Investigating the Impact of Resource Focus and Resource Valence

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses how employees’ emotional and behavioral investments in organizations—specifically affective commitment and citizenship behavior—are influenced by the trickle-down of organizational inclusiveness through supervisors. While prior research highlights the value of inclusive environments, less is known about how inclusiveness propagates across organizational levels. The authors identify a gap in understanding the psychological mechanisms that enable or constrain this transmission, particularly the role of supervisor characteristics. They propose that supervisory inclusiveness mediates the effect of organizational inclusiveness on employee outcomes, and that supervisors’ moral identity moderates this process. Drawing on social cognitive theory, they test this model using a 2×2 experiment and a multi-source field study. Their contribution lies in demonstrating a moderated mediation mechanism that explains variability in how inclusiveness spreads within organizations.

title: Improving employee emotional and behavioral investments through the trickle-down effect of organizational inclusiveness and the role of moral supervisors

entries.rq_with_context: As more autistic individuals enter the workforce, there is growing need to understand their workplace experiences from an organizational perspective. Existing research is limited and often relies on disability-focused theories rather than inductive, organizationally grounded insights. This study addresses the gap by exploring how autism influences key employment areas—hiring, job performance, and leadership—through the lived experiences of autistic employees and their managers. The research asks three questions: What are the shared tensions during hiring? On the job? And in manager-employee interactions? Using grounded theory with written responses from two samples, the authors inductively develop a framework centered on disclosure-related tensions. The contribution is a bottom-up understanding of autism at work that highlights mutual perspectives and practical implications for inclusive management.

title: Tensions on the spectrum: an inductive investigation of employee and manager experiences of autism

entries.rq_with_context: Newcomer socialization is critical for organizational commitment and retention, yet the psychological mechanisms underlying effective adjustment remain understudied. While prior research links institutionalized socialization tactics and supervisor support to positive outcomes, the role of basic psychological need satisfaction—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—as a mediating mechanism has not been systematically examined. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study investigates how socialization tactics and perceived autonomy support from supervisors jointly influence newcomers’ need satisfaction, which in turn affects their affective commitment and withdrawal cognitions. Using a time-lagged survey of 489 MBA interns, we apply structural equation modeling to test an integrated model. The study contributes by identifying need satisfaction as a central psychological mechanism linking organizational and supervisory inputs to key socialization outcomes.

title: Satisfying Newcomers’ Needs: The Role of Socialization Tactics and Supervisor Autonomy Support

entries.rq_with_context: Innovation is critical for organizational success, and work teams are increasingly central to innovation efforts. While charismatic leadership is thought to foster innovation, findings have been inconsistent, possibly due to unexamined mediating and moderating mechanisms. This study investigates whether team potency mediates the relationship between charismatic leadership and team innovative behavior, and whether task interdependence moderates this mediation. Using a three-wave longitudinal design with multi-source data from 133 Spanish bank branches, the study applies structural equation modeling to test these relationships at the team level. The authors aim to uncover the psychological mechanism and boundary conditions underlying charismatic leadership’s impact on team innovation, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of leadership effectiveness in team contexts.

title: Charismatic Leadership and Work Team Innovative Behavior: the Role of Team Task Interdependence and Team Potency

entries.rq_with_context: Accurate data collection is critical in behavior analysis, but human error—especially delayed recording—can compromise data quality and lead to poor treatment decisions. Electronic data collection (EDC) systems offer promise by providing automated prompts and feedback, potentially replacing supervisory oversight. However, little research has examined which specific components of such systems are effective. This study fills that gap by conducting a component analysis of an EDC system to identify how automated prompts and different types of feedback influence data collection timeliness among caregivers working independently. Using a single-case design, the authors test each component individually. They claim the study contributes to understanding how technology can support data fidelity in real-world, unsupervised settings.

title: A Component Analysis of an Electronic Data Collection Package

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback is widely used to improve employee performance, but there is inconsistency in research about its effectiveness, possibly due to unexamined differences in how feedback is delivered. While objective feedback provides measurable data on past performance, little research has compared the impact of different delivery methods such as computer displays, text messages, or face-to-face interactions. This study addresses this gap by evaluating how feedback modality affects performance in a controlled laboratory setting using a check-entering task. The authors employed a between-group repeated measures design with random assignment to one of four conditions: no feedback, computer-delivered feedback, text message feedback, or face-to-face feedback. The primary contribution is identifying that face-to-face delivery leads to significantly better performance compared to no feedback, while other modalities did not differ significantly from control.

title: The Effects of Feedback Modality on Performance

entries.rq_with_context: The Performance Diagnostic Checklist-Human Services (PDC-HS) is an informant-based tool used by consultants to identify variables affecting employee performance in human service organizations. While prior research demonstrated its validity and reliability using scripted video vignettes, those scenarios may lack real-world applicability. This study addresses that gap by using transcribed interviews from actual PDC-HS consultations to create more authentic video scenarios. The research question is whether the PDC-HS remains valid and reliable when assessed with these realistic vignettes. Using a repeated-measures design with three videos indicating one, two, or three problematic domains, the study evaluates validity through scoring accuracy and reliability via test–retest and interrater agreement. The key contribution is providing further evidence of the tool’s psychometric properties under conditions closer to actual practice.

title: Further Evaluation of the Validity and Reliability of the Performance Diagnostic Checklist-Human Services

entries.rq_with_context: In human service settings like applied behavior analysis (ABA), frontline staff often fail to implement key procedures such as contriving opportunities for mand training, which is critical for client learning. While tools exist to diagnose causes of poor performance, there is limited research applying these tools to complex, clinically significant behaviors in community-based settings. The study uses the PDC-HS to assess why three behavior instructors perform poorly on mand training and whether the recommended intervention—behavioral skills training (BST)—improves their performance. Using a multiple baseline design across participants, the authors evaluate BST’s effectiveness. The study claims to replicate and extend prior findings by demonstrating the utility of the PDC-HS in real-world, home-based ABA services.

title: Utilizing the Performance Diagnostic Checklist – Human Services to Assess and Improve Employee Performance on Mand Training: A Replication

entries.rq_with_context: Human services organizations often struggle with financial sustainability, yet pay-for-performance (PFP) systems—where compensation is tied directly to output—have been rarely studied in this sector despite their demonstrated effectiveness in other fields. Existing research shows PFP can improve performance, but gaps remain regarding its feasibility and effects in service-based, non-profit settings where work outputs are harder to quantify. This paper addresses that gap by implementing and evaluating a PFP system in a behavioral health clinic’s consultation department staffed by behavior analysts. The research question is whether transitioning from conventional fixed pay to a PFP model increases billable service hours and improves net profit. The study uses an A-B-C design across three phases: baseline (standard pay), process intervention, and PFP. The contribution lies in demonstrating a practical application of PFP in a human services context, including financial modeling, implementation steps, and social validity data.

title: An Application of Pay-for-Performance in a Human Services Setting

entries.rq_with_context: Illegal parking on university campuses is a persistent problem that contributes to student frustration and has been linked to attrition, especially among first-generation and non-traditional students. While universities commonly use citations to deter illegal parking, these punitive measures may increase negative feelings toward the institution without fully addressing the underlying causes, such as confusion about parking rules. Prior research shows that informational signs and citizen-led warnings can reduce illegal parking, but few studies have combined direct performance feedback with enforcement. This study investigates whether adding performance feedback—via sticky notes placed on illegally parked vehicles—reduces illegal parking more effectively than citations alone. Using a reversal design across four semesters, the authors measure changes in illegal parking rates during baseline, treatment, and reversal phases. The study contributes by demonstrating a low-cost, behavior-analytic intervention that complements traditional enforcement.

title: Using Prompts and Feedback to Reduce Illegal Parking in a University Parking Lot

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback is widely used to improve performance in organizational settings, but less is known about how specific dimensions like accuracy and timing influence its effectiveness. While prior research shows accurate feedback improves performance and immediate feedback is generally better than delayed feedback, no study has examined how accuracy and timing interact. This study addresses that gap by testing the combined effects of feedback accuracy (100%, 80%, 20%) and timing (trial-by-trial vs. block feedback) on skill acquisition using a computerized match-to-sample task with undergraduate students. The authors use a 2 × 3 factorial design to compare performance across conditions. They find that accuracy significantly affects performance, while timing does not, and there is no interaction between the two.

title: Examining the Effects of Feedback Accuracy and Timing on Skill Acquisition

entries.rq_with_context: While extensive research exists on delivering feedback to improve workplace performance, little to no empirical attention has been paid to how employees receive feedback, despite anecdotal evidence that employee behavior during feedback sessions may influence its effectiveness. Existing nonempirical sources suggest certain behaviors—like active listening and acknowledging mistakes—may help, but these have not been systematically tested or taught using behavioral methods. This study addresses this gap by developing a set of observable feedback-receiving skills and testing whether they can be taught using behavioral skills training (BST). Using a nonconcurrent multiple-baseline design across three participants, the researchers evaluated skill acquisition and maintenance. The primary contribution claimed is the initial development and preliminary evaluation of a teachable repertoire for receiving feedback, representing a novel direction in organizational behavior management.

title: Teaching Employees How to Receive Feedback: A Preliminary Investigation

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback and praise are commonly used in organizational behavior management, and while research has examined employee preferences for feedback format, little is known about how those preferences change over time. Existing studies typically assess preference at a single point, ignoring potential shifts due to repeated exposure. This study addresses the gap by evaluating whether preference for feedback-related stimuli changes after repeated exposure to high- and low-effort tasks. Drawing on the basic literature on within-trial contrast, it asks whether stimuli signaling work become less preferred and whether praise stimuli following work become more preferred—especially after higher-effort tasks. Using a simulated work task with an FR1 vs. FR20 schedule, the study measures changes in preference through repeated paired-stimulus assessments. It contributes to OBM by exploring how the timing and effort context of feedback delivery may shape employee preferences over time.

title: The Role of Effort in Shifting Preference for Feedback Stimuli

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback is a widely used tool in organizational behavior management, and it is generally assumed that feedback must be accurate to improve performance. However, in practice, supervisors may provide inaccurate feedback—either due to lack of monitoring or intentional bias—and workers may or may not detect this inaccuracy. Prior research suggests that when workers are unaware of inaccuracy, inaccurate feedback may still be effective, but when they are aware, it may undermine performance. This study investigates the role of awareness by manipulating whether participants can visibly see the outcomes of their work. It asks: does inaccurate feedback affect performance differently when performance outcomes are visible versus non-visible? Using a simulated task with a 2x2 experimental design, the study tests performance under accurate/inaccurate feedback and visible/non-visible conditions. The contribution is empirical evidence that visibility of performance outcomes (as a proxy for awareness) moderates the effectiveness of feedback accuracy.

title: Effects of Accurate and Inaccurate Feedback on Work Performance: The Role of the Awareness of Inaccuracy

entries.rq_with_context: Tailgating, or following too closely, is a major contributor to rear-end crashes, yet many drivers misestimate their following headway and fail to maintain safe distances. Prior research has shown interventions can improve following headway in simulators, but effects often do not maintain. This study fills a gap by evaluating a comprehensive package intervention—including self-monitoring and education—aimed at increasing following headway among young drivers in a simulator, assessing maintenance during a reversal phase, and testing whether gains transfer to real-world driving. The study uses a non-concurrent multiple baseline design with three participants. The authors claim the study contributes by demonstrating both maintenance and real-world transfer of improved following headway using a behavioral intervention.

title: Increasing Following Headway in a Driving Simulator and Transfer to Real World Driving

entries.rq_with_context: Educational services for children with autism in China vary in quality, and organizational behavior management (OBM) and performance management (PM) practices remain underdeveloped in this context. Despite evidence supporting PM components like training, monitoring, and feedback in Western settings, these methods have not been systematically introduced or evaluated in Chinese autism agencies. The study investigates whether using a consultant workshop model—training managers to implement a structured PM system—can improve teacher performance across multiple domains of ABA instruction. The approach follows a preliminary quasi-experimental A-B design across four agencies, measuring changes in teaching fidelity. The authors claim the study offers initial evidence for the cross-cultural applicability of OBM methods in improving service delivery in non-Western, resource-limited contexts.

title: Using a Consultant Workshop Model to Improve Performance Management in Chinese Autism Agencies: A Preliminary Study

entries.rq_with_context: In organizational settings, time-based pay systems often lack contingency between performance and reinforcement, leading to lower productivity and job satisfaction. Contingent-pay systems may improve performance, but questions remain about how best to structure them—specifically, whether using high-preference versus varied reinforcers and fixed-ratio (FR) versus variable-ratio (VR) schedules affects outcomes. Prior research shows mixed results regarding varied reinforcers and schedule types, with some evidence favoring high-preference and VR schedules. This study addresses gaps by examining the effects of both consequence quality and schedule type on performance and preference in a laboratory setting. Using a reversal design with a multielement component and concurrent-chains preference assessment, the authors evaluate responding under four conditions: FR/HiP, VR/HiP, FR/Varied, and VR/Varied. The contribution is a preliminary comparison of how these combined parameters influence performance and choice in a simulated workplace task.

title: A Preliminary Laboratory Evaluation: Effects of Consequence Quality and Ratio-Schedule Arrangements on Staff Performance

entries.rq_with_context: The demand for certified behavior analysts has risen sharply, creating challenges for organizations trying to hire qualified staff. While employers commonly use exhibit booths at conferences and career fairs—and often provide small free gifts—there is no published evidence on whether such giveaways actually influence recruitment outcomes. Existing literature recommends these practices, but their empirical effects are unknown. This study addresses that gap by asking: Does providing free items at a recruitment booth increase the number of attendees who verbally contact a recruiter or leave an email for follow-up? Using an alternating-treatments design across three events, the researchers compared conditions with and without giveaways. They found that giveaways significantly increased verbal contacts but did not significantly increase email sign-ups, suggesting they attract attention but may not boost serious job interest.

title: Hiring Behavior Analysts: Free Gifts at a Booth Increase Verbal Contacts with a Recruiter, but Not Serious Job Inquiries

entries.rq_with_context: Communication and situational awareness are critical skills in high-reliability organizations like healthcare, yet objective methods for assessing them remain limited. While TeamSTEPPS® is widely used to improve these skills, there is little empirical assessment of its impact using precise behavioral measures. This study addresses this gap by using virtual reality (VR) simulations combined with verbal coding and eye-tracking to assess the effects of TeamSTEPPS® training on communication accuracy and observing responses among medical and nursing students. A pre/post design was used with a VR emergency simulation involving an eclamptic seizure scenario. The study contributes a technical feasibility demonstration of integrating VR with behavioral measurement tools to objectively evaluate training outcomes.

title: Using Virtual Simulations to Assess Situational Awareness and Communication in Medical and Nursing Education: A Technical Feasibility Study

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly use technology to deliver feedback, but the effectiveness of different methods may depend on social dynamics like authority relations. While feedback is known to improve performance, less is known about how its impact varies based on who delivers it and how, especially when considering established authority relationships. This study addresses this gap by testing performance under four feedback conditions: authority face-to-face, authority email, non-authority face-to-face, and non-authority email. Using a simulated work task with 120 participants, the authors compare performance across these conditions. They find that both feedback methods work well with authority figures, but only face-to-face feedback is effective with non-authority figures. The study contributes by showing that the social relationship between provider and recipient moderates the effectiveness of feedback delivery method.

title: The Impact of Authority Relations and Feedback Delivery Method on Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Research has long explored workplace stressors, but recent work distinguishes between challenge stressors (e.g., workload, responsibility) that may offer growth potential and hindrance stressors (e.g., role ambiguity, politics) that hinder goal attainment. While prior studies suggest challenge stressors benefit performance and reduce turnover, findings are mixed, especially regarding personality's role. The authors identify a gap in understanding how conscientiousness—often seen as a protective trait—interacts with these stressors. Using conservation of resources (COR) and personal resource allocation (PRA) theories, they test whether conscientiousness acts as a resource allocator in shaping responses to stress. Their research question asks how conscientiousness moderates the effects of challenge and hindrance stressors on psychological strain, turnover intentions, and job performance in a Pakistani sample. They use a time-lagged, multi-source design to improve causal inference.

title: Challenge-Hindrance Stressors and Job Outcomes: the Moderating Role of Conscientiousness

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the widespread use of workplace coaching, there is limited understanding of how specific coaching practices and coachee job characteristics influence coaching outcomes. While prior research has shown coaching to be effective overall, less is known about how factors like coaching format (e.g., face-to-face vs blended) or coach origin (internal vs external) affect distinct outcome types such as work well-being versus personal effectiveness. Additionally, little attention has been paid to whether job complexity shapes coaching effectiveness. This study addresses these gaps by examining survey data from 161 coachees to determine how coaching practice factors and job complexity relate to two outcome criteria. Using regression and interaction analyses, the authors test four hypotheses. The study contributes by showing that coaching effectiveness varies depending on outcome type, coaching approach, and coachee job context, particularly through the interaction of external coaching and high job complexity.

title: Boundary conditions of workplace coaching outcomes

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly rely on intrapreneurial employees, particularly young ones, to drive innovation from the bottom up. While management support is known to be crucial for intrapreneurship, direct supervisors have received little attention in this context. There is limited understanding of what young intrapreneurs specifically expect from their leaders, despite evidence that unmet expectations can harm performance and engagement. This study investigates two research questions: (1) What do young employees in intrapreneurial jobs expect from their leaders? and (2) Which aspects of the full-range leadership theory do they expect most? Using qualitative group interviews with 42 intrapreneurs and 13 leaders in a Dutch IT consultancy firm, the study applies grounded theory and analyzes data through the lens of Implicit Leadership Theory and full-range leadership theory. The authors claim contributions to understanding leadership expectations in intrapreneurial contexts, expanding ILT research, and highlighting the importance of differentiating subdimensions of transformational leadership.

title: You can't always get what you want? Leadership expectations of intrapreneurs

entries.rq_with_context: Supervisor self-interested behavior (SIB), such as taking credit for others' work or using organizational resources for personal gain, threatens employee well-being and undermines workplace exchange relationships. While prior research has focused on why leaders engage in SIB, less is known about its downstream effects on employees and the conditions under which these effects occur. This study addresses that gap by examining how perceived supervisor SIB reduces employees’ affective commitment to their supervisor (ACS), leading to increased counterproductive work behavior toward individuals (CWBI) and the organization (CWBO). Using social exchange theory, the authors propose that when employees perceive unfair treatment, they reciprocate negatively, especially if they have low power distance orientation (PDO). The study uses a two-wave survey with multilevel path analysis across 146 workgroups in six Chinese firms. Its main contribution is identifying ACS as a mediating mechanism and PDO as a boundary condition in the relationship between perceived SIB and employee CWB.

title: Consequences of supervisor self-interested behavior: a moderated mediation

entries.rq_with_context: Despite widespread telework policies, actual telework usage remains low, largely due to manager resistance. Prior research identifies trust as a key barrier, but lacks quantitative assessment of its relative importance compared to other factors such as job interdependence, media richness, equity norms, and employee commuting demands. This paper addresses this gap by testing an integrative model that compares the impact of trust-related judgments against these alternative considerations in managers’ telework decisions. Using two studies—one policy-capturing experiment and one field survey—the authors examine which factors most strongly predict telework allowance. The key contribution is demonstrating that interpersonal trust and perceptions of employee conscientiousness dominate over other theoretically relevant factors, even when structural or technological supports exist.

title: Unpackaging Manager Mistrust in Allowing Telework: Comparing and Integrating Theoretical Perspectives

entries.rq_with_context: Despite extensive research on organizational change, many initiatives fail due to lack of employee support. While information and participation are commonly recommended to foster support, their effectiveness is inconsistent. This study investigates how these practices affect employee support during a building relocation, using the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) to explain underlying mechanisms—attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. It also tests whether high job demands (e.g., role overload) reduce the effectiveness of these practices. The contribution lies in demonstrating that change management practices work primarily through TPB variables, but only when job demands are low or moderate.

title: Too Busy to Change: High Job Demands Reduce the Beneficial Effects of Information and Participation on Employee Support

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates how various safety-specific leadership behaviors—both active (transformational, contingent reward, management-by-exception active) and passive/avoidant (management-by-exception passive, laissez-faire)—affect employee safety motivation. While leadership is recognized as a key factor in workplace safety, little research has examined the range of leader behaviors or the psychological mechanisms linking them to motivation. Moreover, prior studies often rely on cross-sectional designs, limiting causal inference. This study addresses these gaps by using a prospective two-wave design with a 3-month interval and applying the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) to test attitudes, norms, and perceived control as mediators. The main research question is: How do safety-specific leader behaviors relate to safety motivation, and to what extent are these relationships mediated by attitudes, norms, and perceived control toward safety behaviors? The study contributes by being the first to simultaneously examine multiple leader behaviors and their underlying processes in predicting safety motivation.

title: Examining Attitudes, Norms, and Control Toward Safety Behaviors as Mediators in the Leadership-Safety Motivation Relationship

entries.rq_with_context: Prevention focus has been linked both positively and negatively to counterproductive work behavior (CWB), creating an inconsistent literature. Some studies suggest it increases CWB due to heightened negative emotions like anxiety, while others suggest it reduces CWB because it strengthens employees’ sense of obligation to follow rules. This paper addresses the gap by testing both affective (negative emotions) and cognitive (felt obligations) mechanisms simultaneously. The research question is whether and how prevention focus relates to CWB through these dual pathways. Using regulatory focus theory, the authors test a dual-mediation model across two multi-wave studies. The contribution lies in clarifying the conflicting findings by identifying distinct mechanisms that differentially influence types of CWB.

title: Opposing Affective and Cognitive Effects of Prevention Focus on Counterproductive Work Behavior

entries.rq_with_context: The U.S. spends more on healthcare than any other country, yet quality remains below average, prompting a shift from fee-for-service to value-based care, where hospitals are reimbursed based on quality metrics. Despite this shift, many critical processes in healthcare—such as infection control, patient safety, and clinical compliance—are inconsistently followed, with employee behavior being a central factor. The paper seeks to assess how OBM, which applies behavioral principles to improve workplace performance, has contributed to healthcare quality thus far and identifies opportunities for future research. Using the four domains of value-based purchasing (clinical processes, patient experience, outcomes, efficiency), the authors review existing OBM applications and propose areas for expansion. The contribution lies in framing OBM as a scalable, evidence-based approach to help hospitals meet value-based care goals.

title: A Paradigm Shift in Healthcare: An Open Door for Organizational Behavior Management

entries.rq_with_context: In modern work environments, teams are central to organizational success, and employees are expected to be engaged and creative. Job autonomy is generally seen as a resource that enhances motivation, engagement, and creativity. However, prior research shows mixed results, suggesting that contextual and individual factors may alter its effectiveness. This study investigates whether team-level performance pressure and individual learning goal orientation moderate the relationship between job autonomy and individual outcomes. Using multilevel modeling with data from Chinese teams, the authors test both two-way and three-way interactions. The key contribution is identifying boundary conditions under which autonomy either enhances or fails to improve engagement and creativity, particularly highlighting the role of team-level pressures and personal goal orientations.

title: Exploring the Effects of Job Autonomy on Engagement and Creativity: The Moderating Role of Performance Pressure and Learning Goal Orientation

entries.rq_with_context: Employees face different types of job stressors—challenge stressors like job complexity that can enhance motivation, and hindrance stressors like role conflict that tend to undermine it. While prior research has linked these stressors to work outcomes, less attention has been paid to the cognitive appraisals that mediate these relationships, especially in field settings over time. This study addresses this gap by examining how employees' appraisals of job complexity and role conflict mediate their effects on motivation and persistence, using a time-lagged design with data collected over four months. It further explores how task efficacy—the belief in one’s ability to perform job tasks—moderates both the appraisal process and the indirect effects of stressors on motivation. The study contributes by testing a moderated mediation model grounded in transactional theory of stress, offering insight into individual differences that shape stressor appraisals and downstream motivational outcomes.

title: Stressors and Stressor Appraisals: the Moderating Effect of Task Efficacy

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational wrongdoing can harm employees, organizations, and the public, yet many employees hesitate to report it due to fear of retaliation. While prior research has examined individual and organizational factors affecting whistle-blowing, the role of perceived ethical climate remains underexplored. This paper addresses that gap by investigating how perceived ethical climate affects internal whistle-blowing intention through psychological mechanisms rooted in social identity theory. The authors propose that organizational identification and moral identity mediate the effect of ethical climate, while individual risk aversion moderates these relationships. Using a two-wave survey of 667 Chinese employees, they test five hypotheses using hierarchical regression analysis. The study contributes by uncovering the 'black box' of psychological mechanisms linking ethical climate to whistle-blowing and identifying risk aversion as a boundary condition.

title: Psychological mechanisms linking ethical climate to employee whistle-blowing intention

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses the ongoing debate about whether very difficult goals continue to enhance performance or if there is a threshold beyond which they become counterproductive.
