However, intermediary platform firms like Uber or Deliveroo design and implement HRM activities—such as performance management, workforce planning, and compensation—while legally avoiding employer status and denying employment relationships with gig workers. This creates a paradox: HRM practices exist without employment ties, raising questions about how HRM should be conceptualized in this new context. The authors address this gap by proposing an ecosystem perspective that shifts the focus from dyadic employment relations to multilateral exchanges among gig workers, requesters, and platforms. They argue that HRM in this setting serves to govern platform ecosystems by aligning these actors’ interactions to ensure value co-creation. Their contribution is a theoretical framework that redefines HRM’s role and offers propositions for future research on its design and implementation in gig economy ecosystems.

title: Conceptualizing human resource management in the gig economy: Toward a platform ecosystem perspective
Moving Forward: Welcoming the New Editor of the Journal of Organizational Behavior Management

entries.rq_with_context: Work motivation research has shown that both conscious and subconscious (primed) goals can influence performance, but most priming studies have been lab-based or limited to nonprofit call centers using photographs as primes. A key gap exists in demonstrating the real-world applicability of goal priming in for-profit organizations using natural managerial communication. This paper addresses that gap by testing whether a CEO's email containing achievement-related words can unconsciously prime performance goals and improve employee effectiveness and efficiency. Using a field experiment followed by a conceptual replication in the lab, the authors test both performance outcomes and motivation as a mediating mechanism. The approach is grounded in goal setting theory (GST), extending it to subconscious processes. The claimed contribution is twofold: demonstrating the practical utility of verbal priming in organizational leadership communication and identifying motivation as a mediator of primed goal effects.

title: Prime and Performance: Can a CEO Motivate Employees Without Their Awareness?

entries.rq_with_context: Work-family conflict (WFC) is widely studied, and while researchers agree on its conceptual definition (Greenhaus & Beutell, 1985), there is no consensus on how to measure it. Numerous WFC scales exist that differ in content domain, number of items, and response format, yet they are often treated as interchangeable. This assumption may contribute to inconsistent findings across studies. The paper investigates whether four commonly used WFC scales—Carlson et al. (2000), Netemeyer et al. (1996), Grzywacz et al. (2006), and Fisher et al. (2016)—yield comparable results. Using both classical test theory (CTT) and item response theory (IRT), the authors examine whether these scales relate to the same higher-order construct and whether their use leads to systematically different correlations with established correlates. The key contribution is demonstrating that scale choice meaningfully impacts observed relationships and measurement precision, urging greater care in scale selection.

title: Psychometric Evaluation of Work-Family Conflict Measures Using Classic Test and Item Response Theories

entries.rq_with_context: Performance ratings are commonly used as criteria in personnel selection validation, but they often exhibit clustering due to supervisors rating multiple subordinates, leading to non-independent data. This nested structure introduces rater variance that may bias validity estimates downward, yet researchers lack practical methods to correct for this when only one rater per ratee is available. Existing corrections rely on interrater reliability, which requires multiple raters per employee—unavailable in fully nested designs. This paper addresses the gap by simulating nested validation scenarios to quantify the attenuation of validity coefficients due to rater variance. The research asks: (1) How much are observed validity coefficients attenuated under different levels of rater variance? (2) How do sample size and ratee-to-rater ratios influence this attenuation? (3) Can a correction based on ICC(1) recover the true validity? Using simulation, the study models various ICC(1) levels, population validities, sample sizes, and group sizes. The key contribution is demonstrating both the severity of attenuation in typical nested designs and evaluating ICC(1) as a viable post hoc correction method when traditional reliability estimates are unavailable.

title: I Only Have One Rater Per Ratee, So What? The Impact of Clustered Performance Rating Data on Operational Validity Estimates

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly adopt shared workspaces to foster collaboration and reduce costs, yet evidence on their actual impact—especially for knowledge workers—is mixed. While such spaces are expected to enhance communication and innovation, prior research shows they may increase distraction, reduce privacy, and harm well-being. This study addresses a gap in experimental research by using a panel design to evaluate how transitioning to shared workspaces affects knowledge workers’ perceptions and self-reported performance. The research question is whether shared workspaces increase job demands (e.g., distraction, lack of privacy) and decrease job resources (e.g., collaboration, networking), and how these factors relate to productivity. Using a quasi-experimental panel design with pre- and post-move surveys, the study compares those who moved to shared spaces with those who remained in private offices or stayed in shared ones. Its key contribution is isolating the effect of office type from the effect of relocation, thereby controlling for the Hawthorne effect and providing clearer causal evidence.

title: Perceptions and performance of knowledge workers transitioning from single-cell offices to shared workspaces: evidence from panel data

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates how individual differences in core self-evaluation (CSE) influence employee creativity. While prior research links personality traits to workplace creativity, less is known about the mechanisms through which CSE affects creative outcomes. The authors identify knowledge sharing and work meaningfulness as two potential mediators that may explain this relationship. Using a two-wave data collection design with employee and supervisor reports, they test a moderated mediation model. The study contributes by uncovering the psychological and behavioral processes that connect CSE to creativity in organizational settings.

title: Correction to: Linking Core Self-Evaluation to Creativity: the Roles of Knowledge Sharing and Work Meaningfulness

entries.rq_with_context: The paper explores how employees' perceptions of their immediate workspace and broader workplace environment influence organizational citizenship behaviors (OCBs). While prior research has linked office design and ambient features to employee well-being, less is known about how both proximal (e.g., lighting, acoustics) and distal (e.g., green spaces, building aesthetics) environmental factors jointly affect discretionary employee behaviors. This study addresses that gap by testing the effects of IWS and EWQ on OCBs, using social exchange theory and environmental psychology as guiding frameworks. The authors propose that IWS and EWQ enhance POS and engagement, which in turn increase OCBs. Using survey data from 1,206 U.S. full-time workers, they test a structural model with half the sample for scale validation and half for hypothesis testing. The key contribution is distinguishing between two types of workplace perceptions and demonstrating their differential mediating pathways to OCBs.

title: Relationship of immediate workspace and environmental workplace with organizational citizenship behaviors

entries.rq_with_context: Overqualified employees—those with more education, skills, or experience than their jobs require—often face negative work outcomes like withdrawal and turnover intention. Prior research shows that job autonomy can buffer these effects, but it remains unclear how autonomy exerts this benefit. The key gap is understanding the behavioral mechanism linking autonomy to improved outcomes for overqualified individuals. This study proposes that job crafting—the proactive reshaping of job tasks and relationships—is the process through which autonomy translates into positive outcomes. Using a multisource sample of 226 employee-supervisor dyads, the authors test whether job crafting mediates the moderating effect of autonomy on the relationship between overqualification and both withdrawal and turnover intention. Their contribution lies in uncovering the 'how' behind autonomy’s protective role, advancing theoretical understanding of person-environment fit and proactivity in the context of overqualification.

title: The Power of Doing: How Job Crafting Transmits the Beneficial Impact of Autonomy Among Overqualified Employees

entries.rq_with_context: Performance appraisal interviews are critical for feedback and development but remain challenging for both supervisors and employees. While leader empathy is theorized to improve these interactions, little empirical work identifies the specific behaviors that constitute empathic communication in real-time organizational settings. This study addresses that gap by investigating how objective linguistic behaviors—specifically language style matching—reflect empathic communication styles. Using audio recordings from 48 appraisal interviews, the authors analyze linguistic patterns and link them to observer-rated empathy and employee outcomes. The research asks: How is leader empathy behaviorally manifested through language use, and what are its effects on employee intentions and perceptions? The study uses computational text analysis and observational coding to test these relationships, claiming a contribution by identifying micro-level behavioral markers of empathy and demonstrating their functional impact.

title: Engaging the Hearts and Minds of Followers: Leader Empathy and Language Style Matching During Appraisal Interviews

entries.rq_with_context: The field of organizational behavior management (OBM) has grown over time, with increasing interest reflected in certification requirements and scholarly output. However, prior reviews of research productivity in behavior analysis have largely excluded the Journal of Organizational Behavior Management (JOBM), limiting their relevance to OBM specialists. This omission creates a gap in recognizing key contributors and training programs specific to OBM. To address this, the authors conducted a bibliometric review to identify the most published authors, universities, and organizations in JOBM from 1977 to 2019. They also calculated average citations per year per article for the top 20 authors using Google Scholar. The study aims to help students identify experts and quality training programs, recognize institutional contributions, and highlight the role of organizations in producing OBM research.

title: Ranking of the Most Prolific Authors, Universities, and Organizations in the Journal of Organizational Behavior Management

entries.rq_with_context: Despite progress in gender equity, women remain underrepresented in academia, particularly in STEM fields, often referred to as the 'pipeline problem.' While much research focuses on bias after hiring, less is known about early-stage selection processes like letters of recommendation. This two-part study investigates whether gender differences exist in the use of 'doubt raisers'—phrases that question an applicant’s competence—in recommendation letters (Study 1), and whether these doubt raisers influence evaluation outcomes (Study 2). Using archival data from psychology faculty applications and an experimental design with academic evaluators, the authors analyze both the presence of doubt raisers by applicant gender and their causal impact on ratings. The study contributes by showing that even subtle linguistic biases in early screening tools can disadvantage women, despite controls for objective productivity metrics.

title: Raising Doubt in Letters of Recommendation for Academia: Gender Differences and Their Impact

entries.rq_with_context: Small business owners face various job demands, but how they appraise these demands—as challenges or hindrances—has received limited attention. While existing research categorizes job demands a priori, this study highlights that such classifications may not reflect individual appraisals, especially among entrepreneurs. The gap lies in understanding the dynamic, context-dependent nature of these appraisals. The research asks: Which demands do business owners appraise as challenges? Which as hindrances? And do these appraisals depend on their current resource levels? Using a partially grounded theory approach with 20 in-depth interviews, the study builds on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory to explore appraisal mechanisms. It contributes by showing that appraisals are not fixed but shaped by resource availability and role identities.

title: Understanding business owners’ challenge and hindrance appraisals

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace aggression is a widespread and costly problem that causes significant psychological harm to victims, yet little research has examined what victims can do to mitigate this damage. While humor is often suggested as a coping strategy, there is limited experimental evidence on whether it actually helps victims of aggression. This paper addresses this gap by testing whether humor exposure improves well-being after interpersonal aggression and how this occurs. Drawing on the superiority theory of humor and Lazarus and Folkman’s transactional model of stress, the authors propose that humor restores a victim’s sense of power, thereby improving well-being. Through four experimental studies with diverse samples, they test this mechanism across cultures and perpetrator types.

title: Laughter Is (Powerful) Medicine: the Effects of Humor Exposure on the Well-being of Victims of Aggression

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing research on leader character strengths, little is known about the motivational mechanisms through which leaders influence subordinates' prosocial behaviors like organizational citizenship behavior (OCBI). While prior work assumes more honesty/humility is always better, recent theory suggests excessive virtue may be counterproductive (the 'too-much-of-a-good-thing' principle). This study addresses this gap by testing whether leader honesty/humility has a nonlinear effect on OCBI via subordinate moral identity centrality. Using social cognitive and moral identity theories, the authors propose a mediation model with a curvilinear path from leader honesty/humility to subordinate moral identity centrality. The key contribution is providing empirical evidence for nonlinearity in character-based leadership effects.

title: Leader honesty/humility and subordinate organizational citizenship behavior: a case of too-much-of-a-good-thing?

entries.rq_with_context: As global populations age and more individuals balance eldercare with employment, understanding the multidimensional impacts of informal caregiving on workers has become critical. Existing research spans multiple disciplines but lacks an integrative framework to synthesize findings on how eldercare affects employees, families, organizations, and society. This review identifies a gap in cohesive theoretical modeling that accounts for multilevel predictors (e.g., gender, education, policies) and outcomes (e.g., health, job performance). The authors propose a conceptual model grounded in bioecological systems theory, role theory, social role theory, and the job demands/resources model to organize existing knowledge. Their research question centers on how eldercare and work intersect across levels and over time, identifying key mediators like work/family conflict and moderators such as organizational support. The contribution lies in offering a comprehensive framework to guide future research and practice.

title: Eldercare and Work Among Informal Caregivers: A Multidisciplinary Review and Recommendations for Future Research

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates how coworker interactions affect employee performance, focusing on two forms of coworker-resources—support and exchange—and their indirect impact via psychological flourishing. While prior research acknowledges coworker influence on outcomes, inconsistencies exist regarding direct links to performance, suggesting the need to examine mediating mechanisms. Additionally, boundary conditions like individual differences are rarely specified. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory, the authors test psychological flourishing as a mediator and race as a moderator using survey data from 321 employees. The study contributes by clarifying the indirect pathways through which coworker-resources shape performance and identifying race as a key boundary condition.

title: Coworker influence on employee performance: a conservation of resources perspective

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates how transformational versus transactional leadership influences team creativity, focusing on underlying motivational mechanisms. While prior research links leadership styles to team outcomes, less is known about how shared regulatory foci at the team level might explain these effects. The authors propose that transformational leadership enhances team creativity by fostering a collective promotion focus and team initiative, whereas transactional leadership may suppress creativity through a collective prevention focus. Using path analysis in Study 1, they test a model with two forms of collective regulatory focus as mediators. The key contribution is distinguishing between promotion- and prevention-based collective motivations in explaining leadership effects on creativity.

title: Correction to: Collective aspirations: Collective regulatory focus as a mediator between transformational and transactional leadership and team creativity

entries.rq_with_context: Workforce aging and increasing cognitive job demands are shaping how organizations foster innovation. While job design can promote innovative work behavior (IWB), we know little about how age-related cognitive changes affect this process. Existing research has not clarified whether older employees respond to high cognitive demands the same way younger employees do. This study addresses that gap by investigating how employee age moderates the effects of job complexity and job innovation requirements on IWB. Using a lifespan perspective and multilevel analysis of 336 employee-supervisor dyads, the study tests two moderation hypotheses. It contributes by showing that age meaningfully alters the impact of cognitive job demands on IWB, suggesting job design should be age-sensitive.

title: Age-sensitive job design antecedents of innovative work behavior: The role of cognitive job demands

entries.rq_with_context: Situational judgment tests (SJTs) are widely used in employee selection but are increasingly being 'gamified'—modified with game elements—to improve applicant reactions. However, it is unclear whether such changes affect the psychometric quality of the test. This study addresses a gap in experimental research on how specific game elements—immersion (text, audio, still images, video) and control (high vs low)—impact both applicant reactions (e.g., test attitudes, organizational attractiveness) and construct validity. Using a 2x4 between-subjects experiment with 315 participants, the authors test whether these gamification efforts lead to better reactions without harming measurement quality. The approach is grounded in gamification theory, which posits that game elements influence outcomes through psychological states like engagement. The key contribution is providing empirical evidence on the minimal effects of common gamification strategies in SJTs, showing they neither significantly improve reactions nor harm validity.

title: Gamifying a situational judgment test with immersion and control game elements Effects on applicant reactions and construct validity

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace status is generally seen as beneficial, linked to better performance and compensation. However, little is known about its potential negative consequences. This study addresses this gap by exploring how status can simultaneously encourage and discourage knowledge hiding. The research question is: how does workplace status influence knowledge hiding through the mechanisms of felt obligation to share and feeling envied? Using a dual-path perspective of status attainment, the study tests two opposing mediation pathways. The key contribution is providing empirical evidence for both the positive and negative behavioral consequences of status in organizations.

title: Obligations and feeling envied: a study of workplace status and knowledge hiding

entries.rq_with_context: Charismatic leadership is thought to enhance team innovation, but the mechanisms and boundary conditions remain unclear. Prior research has not fully explained how or when charismatic leadership translates into team-level outcomes through psychological mechanisms like team potency. This study addresses this gap by testing a moderated indirect model in which team potency mediates the effect of charismatic leadership on team innovative behavior, and team task interdependence moderates the strength of the leadership–potency relationship. Using a two-wave dataset from 133 teams, the authors test this model with multilevel analysis. The contribution lies in clarifying the contingent mechanisms through which leadership affects team innovation.

title: Correction to: Charismatic Leadership and Work Team Innovative Behavior: the Role of Team Task Interdependence and Team Potency

entries.rq_with_context: In knowledge-intensive organizations, sharing knowledge is vital yet individuals often resist due to effort, risk, and lack of rewards. Ethical leadership may help overcome this by aligning employees with collective interests, but its role in knowledge sharing remains understudied. While prior research links leadership to knowledge sharing, the mechanisms—especially motivational pathways like organizational concern—and contextual constraints such as impression management climate are not well understood. This study asks: how does ethical leadership influence knowledge sharing, through what mechanism, and under what conditions does this effect break down? Using social learning theory, it tests organizational concern as a mediator and impression management climate as a moderator. The key contribution is identifying both a motivational pathway and a boundary condition that limits ethical leadership’s effectiveness in promoting knowledge sharing.

title: Facilitate Knowledge Sharing by Leading Ethically: the Role of Organizational Concern and Impression Management Climate

entries.rq_with_context: The paper explores how social media content, specifically peers’ career advancement updates on professional SNSs like LinkedIn, influences job search behavior among employed individuals. While prior research has examined social contagion in turnover within organizations, little is known about how such mechanisms operate through external digital platforms. The authors integrate the unfolding model of voluntary turnover and social comparison theory to investigate whether these updates act as 'shocks' that trigger job search. They test this using survey data linked to actual resume submissions (n = 125). The study focuses on two individual-level moderators—perceived employability and job embeddedness—to understand differential responses. The contribution lies in extending social contagion research beyond organizational boundaries into the domain of social media.

title: How peers’ updates on social media influence job search

entries.rq_with_context: Work-to-nonwork integration—enacting work roles during nonwork time—is increasingly common due to technological advances and changing work structures, yet its implications for well-being are mixed. Existing research lacks a comprehensive understanding of the motivational factors driving this behavior. This study addresses that gap by applying the Reasoned Action Approach (RAA) to examine four key antecedents: individual integration preference, injunctive and descriptive norms, and perceived behavioral control. Using a two-wave survey of 748 employees, the authors test how these factors predict actual integration behavior one month later. The approach integrates individual and organizational influences within a well-established behavioral framework. The study contributes by demonstrating the joint predictive power of RAA constructs and highlighting the distinct roles of different types of social norms in boundary management.

title: Understanding Employee Motivation for Work-to-Nonwork Integration Behavior: a Reasoned Action Approach

entries.rq_with_context: Lateness to workplace meetings is a common social transgression that can harm interpersonal relationships and team dynamics. While prior research has explored explanations like excuses and apologies in isolation, little is known about how they compare to each other and to providing no explanation at all. This study addresses this gap by testing how excuse, apology, or no explanation after meeting lateness influences observers’ attitudes and behavioral intentions. Using experimental (Study 1) and survey (Study 2) methods, the authors examine expected work performance and prosocial intentions as outcomes. They also investigate how group complaining and the late person’s history of lateness moderate these effects. The study contributes by clarifying the relative effectiveness of explanation types in a real-world context and integrating group and individual factors into the attributions literature.

title: To Excuse or Not to Excuse: Effect of Explanation Type and Provision on Reactions to a Workplace Behavioral Transgression

entries.rq_with_context: Employees’ feedback-seeking behavior (FSB) is crucial for performance and development, yet it is often limited in practice. While prior research has focused on positive leadership as a facilitator of FSB, less attention has been paid to negative leadership behaviors like abusive supervision. This study addresses that gap by exploring how abusive supervision hinders FSB through its impact on employees’ organizational-based self-esteem (OBSE). Drawing on self-concept theory, the authors propose that abusive supervision undermines OBSE, which in turn reduces FSB. They also examine LMX as a boundary condition, testing whether the strength of the supervisor-subordinate relationship alters this indirect effect. The study uses hierarchical regression and path analysis on dyadic data from 312 employee-supervisor pairs in Chinese firms. The key contribution is revealing the psychological mechanism (OBSE) linking abusive supervision to reduced FSB and showing that high LMX intensifies rather than buffers this harmful effect.

title: How does abusive supervision restrict employees’ feedback-seeking behavior?

entries.rq_with_context: Open science practices are increasingly promoted to address concerns about research integrity and a perceived 'reproducibility crisis' in scientific fields, including organizational research. Despite widespread discussion, many researchers remain uncertain about the legitimacy, efficacy, and practical application of these practices. The paper identifies key questions about open science—such as its definition, benefits, limitations, and barriers to adoption—to clarify misconceptions and guide stakeholders. Using a question-and-answer format, it reviews existing evidence on practices like pre-registration, data sharing, and open access. The authors aim to provide actionable recommendations for researchers, editors, and institutions to foster a more transparent and rigorous research culture.

title: Answers to 18 Questions About Open Science Practices

entries.rq_with_context: Traditional cognitive ability tests are strong predictors of job performance but often yield large subgroup differences by race/ethnicity, creating a diversity-validity tradeoff in personnel selection. Existing tests also face limitations related to test-taker engagement, modality constraints, and reliance on crystallized intelligence. To address these issues, the authors developed G.A.M.E., a gamified working memory assessment grounded in modern cognitive theory. The research questions focus on whether G.A.M.E. is reliable, valid, engaging, exhibits smaller subgroup differences than traditional tests, and functions equivalently across computer and mobile devices. The study uses three empirical studies to validate the tool, drawing on CHC theory and complex span task methodology. The key contribution claimed is a new cognitive assessment that maintains predictive validity while reducing adverse impact and improving candidate experience.

title: New frontiers in cognitive ability testing: working memory

entries.rq_with_context: Office housework—non-promotable tasks often assigned to employees—is prevalent in organizations and may contribute to burnout and career stagnation. Prior research suggests women are disproportionately assigned such tasks, but it remains unclear how this affects burnout and promotion outcomes by gender. This study investigates whether gender moderates the relationship between office housework, burnout, and promotion. Using survey data from a diverse sample of employees, the authors test these relationships through regression analysis. The study aims to clarify how gender shapes the consequences of office housework for employee well-being and advancement.

title: Correction to: Office Housework, Burnout, and Promotion: Does Gender Matter?

entries.rq_with_context: Supervisors play a critical role in authorizing idiosyncratic deals (I-deals), yet little is known about their underlying motives for doing so. While existing research has focused on outcomes of I-deals or structural factors influencing them, there is limited understanding of supervisor-level psychological drivers behind these decisions. This study addresses that gap by examining how supervisors’ personal experiences with I-deals, their exchange ideology, and justice sensitivity affect their willingness to grant I-deals to subordinates. Drawing on March’s logic of appropriateness, the authors propose that supervisors’ decisions are shaped by their recognition of the situation (e.g., having received an I-deal themselves), their identity (e.g., beliefs about reciprocity), and normative rules (e.g., fairness considerations). Using data from 182 supervisor-subordinate dyads, the study tests these relationships through hierarchical modeling. The key contribution is identifying individual-level decision-making factors that explain variation in I-deals authorization, thereby enriching the theoretical foundation of I-deals research beyond structural or relational antecedents.

title: Why Grant I-Deals? Supervisors’ Prior I-Deals, Exchange Ideology, and Justice Sensitivity

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses the lack of an integrated understanding of how both presenteeism and absenteeism are shaped by shared cultural norms in organizations. While prior research has examined absenteeism and presenteeism separately, little is known about how collective norms and values interact to form a broader attendance culture. The authors identify a gap in conceptualizing attendance culture as a unified phenomenon that encompasses both behaviors. Their research questions ask whether different types of attendance cultures exist, how they manifest across organizational layers (artifacts, values, assumptions), and how they relate to organizational handling of absence and presence. Using a qualitative approach with 28 semi-structured interviews, they analyze participants’ perceptions through the GIOIA method. The study contributes by proposing a definition of attendance culture that integrates both absenteeism and presenteeism and identifying empirically grounded archetypes that reflect differing legitimacy judgments.

title: Presenteeism and Absenteeism at Work—an Analysis of Archetypes of Sickness Attendance Cultures

entries.rq_with_context: In the Czech Republic, applied behavior analysis (ABA) services are expanding, but practitioners operate with limited oversight, mentorship, and access to professional development, often working in isolation and facing ethical challenges. Existing BST models typically focus on discrete, observable skills rather than the complex, interlocking behavior chains required of supervisory-level practitioners. This creates a gap in sustainable, generalizable training approaches for independent practitioners in underserved regions. To address this, the study piloted a consultant-delivered, extended-format BST series incorporating modular content, practitioner-driven topics, and a self-assessment checklist. The research question is whether this adapted BST package is socially valid—perceived as acceptable and meaningful—and supports skill application beyond training sessions. The approach uses a mixed-methods design combining BST with self-assessment data collected over time. The authors claim this model offers a feasible framework for professional development in emerging ABA markets.

title: Evaluating a Consultant-Delivered Behavioral Skills Training and Self-Assessment Checklist Package used in the Czech Republic

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates how professional commitment affects team effectiveness in multidisciplinary healthcare teams, a context where professionals bring distinct knowledge and identities. While prior research has explored organizational commitment, less is known about how commitment to one’s profession impacts team processes and outcomes. The authors identify a gap in understanding the mechanisms—particularly cognitive diversity—and the conditions under which professional commitment leads to better performance. They propose that professional commitment increases cognitive diversity by motivating members to advocate their professional perspectives, which in turn enhances team effectiveness, but only when task conflict is present to stimulate critical discussion. Using survey data from 70 UK healthcare teams, they test a moderated mediation model. Their key contribution is demonstrating that professional commitment can positively influence team outcomes through a contingent cognitive pathway.

title: Professional Commitment and Team Effectiveness: A Moderated Mediation Investigation of Cognitive Diversity and Task Conflict

entries.rq_with_context: Psychological entitlement—a stable belief in one's deservingness of unearned rewards—has been linked to negative behaviors in various domains, but its role in negotiation remains understudied. While prior research shows that high aspirations and first offers improve individual outcomes, it is unclear whether entitlement promotes such effective strategies while simultaneously encouraging unethical or contentious approaches. This paper investigates this dual impact, proposing that entitlement functions as a 'social trap' by reinforcing self-serving behaviors at relational and ethical costs. Using three cross-sectional studies with recalled, hypothetical, and planned negotiations (n = 615), the authors test how entitlement predicts negotiation attitudes. They find that entitlement predicts both functional attitudes (aspirations, first offer intentions, self-efficacy) and dysfunctional ones (unethicality, zero-sum mindset, dominance), even after controlling for narcissism, neuroticism, and agreeableness. The key contribution is demonstrating that entitlement uniquely shapes negotiation psychology beyond established personality traits.

title: Getting to Excess: Psychological Entitlement and Negotiation Attitudes

entries.rq_with_context: Expressing a stigmatized identity is a complex decision with potential for both positive and negative outcomes, yet existing research presents conflicting findings. While relationship formation theories suggest disclosure improves connection and well-being, stigma theory warns of social devaluation and discrimination. This study addresses the lack of consensus by conducting a meta-analysis of 65 samples (k = 108) to determine when and for whom stigma expression yields beneficial outcomes. The research question is whether stigma expression leads to more positive intrapersonal, interpersonal, workplace, and non-workplace outcomes, and how these relationships are moderated by stigma characteristics and context. Using meta-analytic techniques grounded in stigma and relationship formation theories, the authors test moderators including visibility, controllability, setting (lab vs. field), and recipient gender. The key claimed contribution is providing the first comprehensive meta-analytic test of when stigma expression is beneficial, resolving theoretical contradictions and identifying boundary conditions.

title: Stigma Expression Outcomes and Boundary Conditions: A Meta-Analysis

entries.rq_with_context: The proper estimation of age, period, and cohort (APC) effects is a long-standing challenge in psychological and social research, particularly when studying generational differences. While cross-temporal meta-analysis (CTMA) has become a popular method for detecting cohort effects by analyzing changes in mean scores over time, it relies on strong theoretical and statistical assumptions that have not been empirically tested. A key unresolved issue is whether CTMA can accurately estimate cohort effects given the inherent confounding of period and cohort influences and its reliance on aggregated data. This study addresses this gap by asking: How well does CTMA estimate known confounded period-cohort effects under varying conditions? Using Monte Carlo simulations, we model population-level APC dynamics and assess CTMA’s ability to recover true effect sizes. The work contributes by providing empirical evidence that CTMA often misestimates these effects—either inflating or deflating them—depending on population variability and effect magnitude.

title: Cross-Temporal Meta-Analysis: A Conceptual and Empirical Critique

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing interest in diversity, research often examines single dimensions of identity in isolation, potentially overlooking the compounded effects of multiple minority memberships. Intersectionality theory suggests that people do not experience their identities separately, yet empirical studies frequently fail to account for layered marginalization. This paper addresses this gap by asking how layered group memberships shape work attitudes in a field sample. Using an intersectional framework, the authors analyze data across various combinations of minority statuses. They contribute by demonstrating the importance of considering multiple, overlapping identities when assessing workplace experiences.

title: How Does Intersectionality Impact Work Attitudes?

entries.rq_with_context: Team cohesion is a dynamic emergent state critical to team effectiveness, yet most research on its relationship with team composition has relied on cross-sectional designs. This gap limits understanding of how compositional factors influence cohesion trajectories. Drawing on theories of interpersonal perception and relationship development, this study investigates how team-level personality (e.g., extraversion, neuroticism, agreeableness) and goal orientation (learning, performance-prove) shape both initial levels and changes in social and task cohesion over time. Using a shortitudinal laboratory design with repeated measures, growth curve modeling is applied to test these relationships. The study contributes by revealing when and how different compositional traits impact cohesion, offering insights into team formation and management across time.

title: Built for unity: assessing the impact of team composition on team cohesion trajectories

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses the gap in understanding how toxic leader traits like narcissistic rage affect employees when considered alongside positive leadership behaviors. While prior research has linked narcissistic leaders to negative employee outcomes, little is known about how supportive actions might buffer these effects. The authors examine whether perceived supervisor political support (SPS) moderates the relationship between supervisor narcissistic rage (SNR) and key work outcomes including job satisfaction, OCB, depressed mood, and work neglect. Using three samples across different professions, they apply hierarchical moderated regression to test their hypotheses. The study contributes by showing that SPS can neutralize the adverse effects of SNR, suggesting that even leaders with antagonistic tendencies may not harm subordinates if they also provide political support.

title: Supervisor narcissistic rage: political support as an antidote

entries.rq_with_context: Employees often hesitate to speak up with ideas because voice behaviors are inherently risky—they may be seen as troublemakers or face negative consequences. While prior research highlights leader-member exchange (LMX) as a key factor in promoting voice, it often relies on social exchange logic, which does not fully explain why employees overcome the fear of speaking up. This paper identifies a gap in understanding the psychological mechanism—specifically, how LMX reduces perceived risk—and how contextual factors like perceived leader power shape this process. Drawing on social information processing theory, the authors ask: How does LMX influence voice through perceived risk, and how does perceived leader power moderate this relationship? They test this model using survey data from employee-supervisor dyads in Chinese organizations. The study contributes by shifting from social exchange to a cognitive processing perspective, clarifying how social cues jointly shape voice decisions.

title: Why do employees speak up? Examining the roles of LMX, perceived risk and perceived leader power in predicting voice behavior

entries.rq_with_context: Handwashing adherence among healthcare staff is critical for infection control, yet performance often remains low. Indirect assessment tools like the Performance Diagnostic Checklist-Safety (PDC-Safety) are used to identify barriers to safe behavior, but prior research did not compare indicated versus non-indicated interventions. This study addresses that gap by evaluating whether interventions aligned with the PDC-Safety’s highest-scoring domain are more effective than those from a low-scoring domain. Using a concurrent multiple baseline design, the authors compared a non-indicated intervention (hand sanitizer access) with an indicated intervention (email prompting) for three behavior therapists. The key contribution is providing evidence that PDC-Safety-guided interventions produce better outcomes when matched to assessed problem domains.

title: Further Evaluation of the Performance Diagnostic Checklist-Safety (PDC-Safety)

entries.rq_with_context: Although goal orientation theory acknowledges both stability and variability in individuals' goal preferences, empirical evidence on within-person variability in dispositional goal orientations remains limited. Prior studies have focused on state or domain-specific goal orientations without establishing longitudinal measurement invariance, making it difficult to interpret true change. This study addresses this gap by examining within-person fluctuations in dispositional goal orientations over five time points during a multi-month language training program with 972 participants. Using latent growth modeling and testing for measurement invariance, the research asks whether these goal orientations vary within individuals over time and whether such variability predicts learning outcomes. The approach integrates longitudinal measurement invariance testing with growth modeling to ensure that observed changes reflect actual construct shifts rather than measurement artifacts. The study contributes by providing direct evidence of within-person variability in dispositional goal orientations and linking this variability to multiple learning outcomes, advancing both theoretical understanding and practical applications in training design.

title: Ebb and Flow of Dispositional Goal Orientations: Exploring the Consequences of Within-Person Variability

entries.rq_with_context: There is a common belief among business professionals that rapport-building improves workplace outcomes, but limited research in behavior analysis has tested this idea. While prior studies have shown that rapport improves client outcomes in clinical settings, no experimental research in organizational behavior management (OBM) has directly examined how rapport-building affects employee productivity or discretionary effort. This study addresses that gap by testing the effects of experimenter-led rapport-building behaviors on undergraduate participants’ performance in a simulated work task and their engagement in an optional follow-up survey. Using an experimental design with a rapport-building group and a control group, the study measures productivity via check-processing accuracy and discretionary effort through multiple survey completion metrics. The authors claim the study contributes the first experimental evidence in behavior analysis that rapport-building can increase both productivity and discretionary effort.

title: The Effects of Engaging in Rapport-Building Behaviors on Productivity and Discretionary Effort

entries.rq_with_context: Social attributes such as emotional intelligence and personality traits are important predictors of job performance, yet most assessments rely on traditional self-report questionnaires. Despite growing use of game-based and video-based assessments in recruitment, little research has evaluated their validity for measuring noncognitive traits. This study addresses this gap by developing and testing three novel assessments: a game-based Emotion Recognition Task, a chatbot-based situational judgment test for Emotion Management, and a video interview for Conscientiousness. Using data from over 1,300 participants, the authors assess convergent and discriminant validity, predictive validity for work performance, adverse impact across demographic groups, and user experience. The approach combines machine learning analysis of video responses with gamified task design grounded in established psychometric frameworks. The study contributes early evidence on the validity and fairness of technology-driven assessment methods for social attributes in selection contexts.

title: The potential of game- and video-based assessments for social attributes: examples from practice

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates how employees’ perceived high-performance HR practices (HPHRP) affect their job engagement and organizational citizenship behavior (OCB), building on social-exchange theory. While prior research has linked HPHRP to organizational outcomes, less is known about the direct effects on individual-level behaviors and the role of employee perceptions. Additionally, few studies have examined how leadership, particularly transformational leadership, may strengthen or weaken these relationships. The research addresses this gap by testing whether transformational leadership moderates the links between perceived HPHRP and employee outcomes in two cultural contexts: the US and South Korea. Using survey data from 268 US and 288 South Korean employees, the authors employ hierarchical regression analysis. They claim the study advances understanding by integrating HR practices, leadership, and cultural context to explain variability in employee responses to HPHRP.

title: The role of perceived high-performance HR practices and transformational leadership on employee engagement and citizenship behaviors

entries.rq_with_context: The participation of women in behavior analysis research has been increasingly examined, but the Journal of Organizational Behavior Management (JOBM) has often been excluded from such analyses. While prior work by McGee et al. (2003) reviewed women's participation in JOBM up to 2000, an update is needed to reflect recent trends. This study fills that gap by analyzing yearly data from 1977 to 2018 on women’s representation across multiple roles—overall authors, first authors, sole authors, empirical article authors, and editorial positions—and examines collaboration patterns by gender. Using bibliometric coding of all relevant articles, the authors assess whether participation has approached parity over time. The paper contributes an updated, fine-grained analysis of gender representation in JOBM, extending prior work by including annual trends, focusing on empirical articles, and identifying top women contributors.

title: Participation of Women in the Journal of Organizational Behavior Management: An Update and Extension

entries.rq_with_context: Women remain less likely than men to emerge as leaders in initially leaderless teams, despite evidence of minimal differences in actual leadership behaviors. While prior research highlights verbal participation as a mediator of gender disparities in emergent leadership, little is known about how specific types of communication—differentiated by orientation (task vs. relations) and expression (agentic vs. communal)—predict leadership emergence across genders. This study addresses this gap by testing whether men and women exhibit different amounts of these behaviors and whether such behaviors are differentially associated with emergent leadership based on the speaker’s gender. Using interaction coding of team meetings, the authors analyze 9,042 verbal acts from 116 students in 41 self-managed teams. The framework draws on social role theory and the backlash effect, distinguishing between actor-level behaviors and observer-level perceptions. The key contribution is demonstrating that although men and women communicate similarly, they receive different leadership rewards for their communication, highlighting the role of perceptual bias over behavioral difference.

title: Same talk, different reaction? Communication, emergent leadership and gender

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational climate research often focuses on single specific climates (e.g., safety or service), yet workplaces likely foster multiple climates simultaneously. Empirical evidence shows strong positive correlations among specific climates, contradicting theoretical assumptions that they may compete. This raises questions about whether these associations reflect real theoretical relationships or methodological artifacts. This study investigates the extent to which overlapping climate perceptions are driven by common method variance (CMV)—from self-report and measurement occasion—and by a general positive climate. Using survey data from 353 MTurk workers across industries, the authors analyze correlations among seven specific climates and test competing explanations via structural equation modeling. The key contribution is disentangling methodological from theoretical causes of climate overlap, informing both climate theory and measurement practices.

title: All of the Above?: an Examination of Overlapping Organizational Climates

entries.rq_with_context: Work–life balance (WLB) research has largely focused on working parents and family-related obligations, often overlooking the experiences of single, childless professionals. In Nigeria, where cultural norms prioritize family responsibilities, single workers may face 'time biases'—organizational assumptions that their non-work time is less valuable. This qualitative study investigates how single Nigerian managers and doctors perceive the fairness of WLB policies and how those perceptions influence their work attitudes. Using organisational justice theory as a framework, it draws on interviews with 44 professionals. The authors argue that recognizing the non-work commitments of singles and addressing cultural and contextual biases in policy implementation constitutes a key contribution to more inclusive WLB research and practice.

title: Time biases: exploring the work–life balance of single Nigerian managers and professionals

entries.rq_with_context: Job insecurity is a prevalent workplace demand that negatively impacts employee well-being and engagement. While existing research has largely focused on individual-level resources within the job demands-resources (JD-R) framework, less is known about how group-level resources like social supportive climate shape these relationships. This study addresses that gap by investigating whether autonomy at the individual level and aggregated social supportive climate at the department level moderate the negative effect of job insecurity on work engagement. Using hierarchical linear modeling on cross-sectional data from 3,812 employees across 116 work units, the study tests a multilevel JD-R model. The authors claim their work extends the JD-R theory by demonstrating that resources operate across levels and interact with demands in a cross-level manner.

title: A multilevel model of job insecurity and engagement

entries.rq_with_context: Work-family conflict is increasingly common, especially among dual-earner couples, yet most research has focused on short-term, individual-level effects on family satisfaction. Less is known about how conflict at the couple level impacts long-term changes in family structure, such as separation or having children. This study addresses that gap by investigating how couple-level work-family conflict influences future family satisfaction and subsequently alters family composition. Using a longitudinal design and resource scarcity theory, it tests whether work-family conflict indirectly predicts couple separation and family expansion via reduced family satisfaction. The study contributes by showing that work-family dynamics can have lasting consequences on the very makeup of families, extending beyond proximal attitudes to behavioral outcomes.

title: All in the Family: the Link Between Couple-Level Work-Family Conflict and Family Satisfaction and Its Impact on the Composition of the Family over Time

entries.rq_with_context: Abusive supervision has harmful effects on employees, yet less is known about its antecedents, especially how both subordinate and supervisor characteristics interact. Prior research often examines these factors in isolation, despite calls to integrate them. This paper addresses that gap by focusing on social value orientation (SVO)—whether individuals are prosocial (concerned with collective welfare) or proself (self-interested). Drawing on the reactive perpetrator–provocative victim model, the authors propose that prosocial supervisors may react negatively to proself subordinates whom they perceive as violating cooperative norms. The research tests whether this dyadic interaction increases abusive supervision and harms in-role performance, using a cross-level moderated mediation model in Study 1 and an experimental scenario in Study 2. The key contribution is demonstrating that 'nice' supervisors can engage in abuse when paired with self-interested subordinates.

title: No more Mr. Nice Guy: social value orientation and abusive supervision
Correction to: Abusive Supervision and Organizational Dehumanization

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates how appreciation influences job satisfaction, building on the 'Stress-as-Offense-to-Self' (SOS) theory, which emphasizes threats or boosts to the self at work. While prior research links appreciation to job satisfaction, less is known about the underlying mechanisms. This paper addresses that gap by testing a longitudinal double-mediation model in which appreciation affects job satisfaction through increased subjective success and reduced organizational resentment. Using a three-wave design with 193 employees from Swiss organizations, the authors analyze data across four months. They find support for the proposed mediation, showing that appreciation not only affirms self-evaluation but also mitigates negative affective reactions. The contribution lies in identifying two distinct psychological pathways through which appreciation operates as a resource.

title: How does appreciation lead to higher job satisfaction?

entries.rq_with_context: Job satisfaction (JS) has long been the dominant measure of job-related well-being, typically defined in hedonic terms as enjoyment derived from work. However, this narrow focus may overlook deeper, eudaimonic aspects of work—such as meaning, purpose, and contribution to one’s life and society. Prior research has critiqued the stagnation in JS conceptualizations, noting that standard measures fail to capture how jobs fulfill broader human needs. This paper addresses that gap by proposing meaning-based job-related well-being (MJW) as an alternative construct. The research question is whether MJW predicts key outcomes—including engagement, inclusion, turnover intention, work-family conflict, and life satisfaction—as well as or better than traditional JS. Using three samples totaling 811 workers, the authors test MJW's distinctiveness and incremental validity using correlational, factor analytic, and regression methods. They find that MJW is related to but distinct from JS and adds significant explanatory power beyond JS, suggesting a broader conceptualization of job satisfaction rooted in the worker’s whole life.

title: Meaning-Based Job-Related Well-being: Exploring a Meaningful Work Conceptualization of Job Satisfaction

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates the combined effects of fear and companionate love—two opposing emotions—on perceptions of leader effectiveness and follower loyalty. While existing research emphasizes the negative consequences of fear and positive effects of love in leadership, this study addresses a gap by exploring how these emotions interact. The authors question whether fear might have beneficial effects when accompanied by love, contrary to prevailing assumptions. Using multi-level modeling and polynomial regression on survey data from a professional services firm, they test if companionate love moderates the impact of fear on leadership outcomes. The study contributes by showing that fear can be positively related to effectiveness and loyalty when paired with high levels of love.

title: Leadership through love and fear: an effective combination

entries.rq_with_context: While self-efficacy is generally seen as positively linked to job performance and creativity, recent research suggests that excessively high self-efficacy may have negative consequences due to complacency and overconfidence. Despite theoretical suggestions of a nonlinear effect, empirical evidence on the curvilinear relationship between self-efficacy and creativity is lacking. This study addresses this gap by testing for an inverted U-shaped relationship between general self-efficacy and employee creativity. Using data from 188 subordinate-supervisor dyads in South Korea, the study further investigates how supervisor close monitoring influences this relationship. The authors draw on social cognitive theory, the Too-Much-of-a-Good-Thing (TMGT) effect, and trait activation theory to frame their hypotheses. The key contribution is providing empirical support for a nonlinear self-efficacy–creativity link and identifying supervisor behavior as a boundary condition.

title: The Curvilinear Relationship between Self-efficacy and Creativity: The Moderating Role of Supervisor Close Monitoring
